I rise, not for the purpose of replying to the hon. gentleman, but merely to correct an omission in the chronological statement I was endeavouring to give of constitutional development. I suggest that the negotiations at Washington in 1911 to which my hon. friend has just alluded, illustrate rather an important development. In the speech from the Throne at the commencement of the session of 1911, reference was made to the desirability of more equitable tariff arrangements between the United States and Canada. Then followed in the Governor General's speech this significant passage:
Following the negotiations which took place some months ago between the President of the United States and my Government the results of which were at the time communicated to Parliament, a further conference between representatives of the two countries has been held ' at Ottawa.
In the first place, the hon. gentleman will notice that allusion is made to negotiations between "the President of the United States and my Government." That certainly is a remarkable advance from the position taken on some of the other occasions to which I have alluded.
Then further on, it is stated that there has been a further conference between representatives of the two countries at Ottawa-not a conference between the representatives of the United Kingdom and of the United States, but between the representatives of Canada and of the United States. My hon. friend's explanation is substantially correct. Mr. Paterson and I went to Washington feeling that we were going to deal with a tariff matter which was clearly within the right of Parliament. When any official from any part of the world comes to Ottawa to discuss any trade arrangement, he naturally comes to the Government of the day, and it would be our right to make an arrangement with him not in the form of a treaty, but in the form of a general understanding. As a matter of courtesy and as a matter of right we called on the British ambassador at once. He understood the matter thoroughly, gave us his blessing, took us to the President and introduced us, and from that time forward we were absolutely free to conduct negotiations, but always with the full knowledge on our part that if those negotiations should eventuate in a treaty, then unquestionably that treaty would (have to be made by the British ambassador, acting in conjunction, as he no doubt would, with the Canadian representative. Whenever you want my help I am here to assist you; but it is your own business". And, as a matter of fact, he took little or no part in the negotiations. Of course, we took care to see, as a matter of courtesy, that he was kept informed. But after all, practically speaking, the whole thing amounts to this, that we cannot make a treaty without the ambassador of Great Britain. We cannot be in the Empire and not accept the responsibilities which that involves. I am not saying anything in a controversial sense, but my view is that we have to-day, in the making of commercial treaties, all the power that we ought to have or that is any good to us. The only thing is that we have no voice in

Imperial affairs, but that is nothing for us to complain of; we can have that voice if we want it; we can have representation in the Imperial Parliament if we desire to be represented there, for no one in England is raising any objection. Anything that we are short of in the way of representation imperially is not due to any action on the part of the Imperial authorities; it is because we have no desire to have that representation. But I do not see that there is anything which we can have in relation to negotiations of treaties which we have not to-day.

Now, if a monarch should wait, before sending his envoys to countries near and far, until important events occur, it will be found that the negotiators sent thus at the eleventh hour on urgent occasions, have no time to explore the .terrain or to study the habits of mind of the foreign court or to create the necessary liaisons or to change the course of events already in flood.

If we are to do our business with our neighbours we must be in constant touch with them, to understand their point of view and to give them the benefit of our point of view, rather than send down an envoy from time to time to settle disputes. Our object should be to so conduct our relations that acute difficulties would not arise. In other \vords, we should endeavour to preserve a good understanding rather than seek to preserve the peace after real difficulties have arisen.

If any question or difference did arise, that would naturally, properly, inevitably, come back to the Government of Canada and the Government of Great Britain and would be settled between them just as all questions are settled from time to time, by conference and negotiation. Trouble would not arise, therefore, in the way my hon. friend has mentioned.
What are the functions of such a minister? He would take part in the negotiation of specific questions arising between the two governments-the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States-acting upon instructions from the Government of Canada, in the same way as a minister would who went down to deal with a specific matter. But in addition, he watches events; when necessary he makes representations to his own government as to the trend or course of events in order that they may anticipate difficulties; and by removing misunderstanding at the outset he may often prevent what would otherwise become a protracted point of differ ence. Then, he transmits to his government from time to time reports of legislation and executive acts. He keeps the Government here fully advised as to what is being done by the Government at Washington-that is a proper function of a diplomatic representative. He also furnishes such general reports as a diplomatic agent sends home with regard to social, industrial and economic questions that may be of interest to his government. He may negotiate treaties if he is instructed by his government to do so, either alone or assisted by a representative sent by his government to co-operate with him.
May I point out that one of the grave difficulties in connection with our present arrangement is the lack of continuity. Every business man knows that if you have important negotiations to carry on, if you have important relations to maintain, continuity of touch, of interest and of sympathy is of the utmost importance; and to

bring this about a permanent representative is necessary. And then, there is the bearing that the personal touch, personal association, has upon the maintaining of good relations. May one draw a lesson from our experience at Geneva? The position at the close of the Assembly was entirely different from that which prevailed at the opening. We did not know each other at the first meeting; we had not sized each other up, so to speak; we had not learned to appreciate each other's point of view. It was only when we got really acquainted with each other, so far as we could in that brief space of time, that business proceeded smoothly and satisfactorily. So that the establishment of personal relation, of personal contact, is of the greatest possible advantage.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has suggested that this arrangement might imperil our relations with the Mother Country. One can only give an opinion, but from my reading of our constitutional history and from the facts of our own experience I would come to an entirely different conclusion. My judgment is that it would not impair but would rather tend to improve the relations not only between Canada and the Mother Country, but also between Canada and the United States. That is the last point that I want to emphasize. One of the most important problems in the world to-day, having regard not only to the relations between the different Anglo-Saxon peoples, but to the peace of the world, is the maintaining of good understanding between the peoples of the British Empire and the United States. Providence has placed us side by side with the great American Republic. In the course of our political development we have retained our connection with the Mother Country, and that enables us to understand their view, their attitude, their ideals and their policies on international questions as the people of the United States, I venture to say, do not understand them. We are able to appreciate the point of view of the Mother Country in a way that the people of the United States do not. On the other hand, our close contact and constant intercourse with the American people enables us to understand them and their ideals in a way, I have no hesitation whatever in saying, that the people of the Mother Country do not understand them. One has only to come in contact with the public men of both nations to appreciate the great importance of each trying to understand the other
and to appreciate the other's point of view. Canada has a unique, a providential opportunity to act as a liason between the two; if we fail to take advantage of it we shall lose one of the greatest opportunities that has ever come to us or ever will come to us to assist in maintaining a good understanding between the British Empire and the United States, not only for the benefit of Canada and the British Empire, but for the peace and progress of the world.
I believe that a Canadian minister at Washington, in touch with the American Government, in constant touch with the British ambassador and in continuous communication with his own Government, would be a means of interpreting one nation to the other so that we may march together, rather than work at cross purposes, toward the attainment of the high ideals which, after all, we do hold in common. Many things do arise which tend to irritate us and to disturb our relations, but fundamentally our ideals are common ideals and it should be our God-given privilege to help bring about whole-hearted co-operation among all branches of the Anglo-Saxon world.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

speechtext: Could my hon. friend give us one or two concrete examples of questions arising specifically between the United States and Canada which would he better handled under the arrangement which he contemplates than they are being handled at the present time?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

speechtext: I will give one. The supply of Canadian pulp and paper to the American press became a very difficult and .acute question. In my humble 'judgment, this possible difficulty might have been wholly avoided if we had a Canadian representative at Washington all the time, watching the situation and keeping the American Government fully informed as to our views and the reasons for our policy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am sure everybody will agree with me that the committee is indebted to the right hon. member for

King's (Sir Robert Borden) and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), for the very excellent and instructive addresses which they gave us this afternoon. I agree with most of what those two hon. gentlemen said; but unfortunately they are, to a certain extent, men of the past in spite of the very eminent position which they occupy in this country, and I should like to know whether my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), who is Minister of External Affairs and who speaks now for the Government and for Canada, agrees with the position taken by both the hon. member for King's and the hon. member for Durham. We have not been fortunate enough to have a statement from the Prime Minister as to this appointment at Washington. Why is it that the appointment has not been made, and why is it that the item which was formerly $80,000 has been reduced to $60,000? Perhaps next year it will be $40,000, and by a slow process of suicide, to use the expression of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), the Government is going to kill its own child.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I was not able to be in the House during all the address of the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden). I am not quite certain, but I think I was present during all the address of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell). I did not hear anything in either address with which I did not agree. I did not hear any sentiments uttered that were at all at variance with my views. There may have been something which I did not altogether catch.
As regards the explanation of the reduction, I am always glad, not only to note, but to explain reductions. This year the War Mission at Washington, which was appointed for the purpose stated by the right hon. member for King's, has been discontinued; it has been wound up. Such purposes as remained after the main purpose was gone, did not seem to me sufficient to warrant the continuance of the office and, consequently, there will not be any office until an appointment, is made to this post. That, however, does not explain the difference in the Estimate, because it is intended to make the appointment. What explains the difference is that there was created-I cannot recall just when, but before the last Estimate was passed a year ago-a press bureau in the city of New York. That has been discontinued as a press bureau. It has been transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce.

As time went on, its work developed more along trade channels than any other; its usefulness was manifestly along those lines. I had an investigation made as to its work and a report made to me verbally by Col. Cooper who was in charge, and as a result, I took the recommendation of each and had that bureau transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce. Twenty thousand dollars is deducted on that account.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I forgot that. I gave it this afternoon to the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). There is one reason and one only, namely that the Government has not been able to decide as to the best man and when I speak of that, I mean available to occupy this very important post.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

May I ask, coming back to this item, whether the $80,000 which was voted last year has been expended, and on what?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: This minister, or ambassador, or plenipotentiary, or whatever he may be, shall be appointed 'by the Crown upon the advice of the Government of Canada, if I correctly understand the statement which was issued last year. It is the Government of Canada that is going to recommend the appointment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: It is stated that in the absence of the British ambassador our Canadian representative will take charge of the British Embassy and will deal with British affairs. Do I understand my right hon. friend to say that the British Government will trust the administration and direction of their foreign affairs in the United States to a Canadian, in the absence of the British ambassador, without having a word to say in his appointment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I think so. They have agreed to the proposal as to the appointment on terms, and one of the terms is that. I do not regard that myself as of first importance. I do not know that there would be any probability of difficulty arising due to that, but if it did, there would be no difficulty in making modifications in that regard. I do not anticipate that there would be difficulty myself, because the British Government would be quite certain that any one recommended by the Government of Canada for a post of that kind would be a man of high responsibility and intimate knowledge of the affairs connected with the embassy. They having assented, I see no reason at all why we might anticipate trouble along that line.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I rise to make my position quite clear in that respect. Any questions I ask are more by way of constructive criticism, because I do not object to the principle. Anything which is a step in the road to nationhood has my full approval. I would like to know whether the, people of Canada will be responsible for the actions of their own appointee when he acts as British ambassador, transacting purely British affairs as distinct from Canadian affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
In as much as he is named on the advice of the Canadian people he would be responsible, I think, in the same way as any other ambassador to
his own country. I do not know what his responsibility to Canada would be in respect to matters purely British. It would appear to me that he would owe direct responsibility in that regard more to Great Britain. He is our direct appointee, and for his general conduct he is responsible to us, but if there are matters which he may be called upon to discharge in this contingency which may never arise, matters in which Canada has no interest but which are purely British, it would appear to me that he would be responsible more directly to the people of Great Britain. They are ready to accept that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
What purpose is
served by this arrangement? Why should it have been agreed that the Canadian representative will act for the British ambassador in his absence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The idea is to give him rank such as he should have. He is in the position second in authority there, and naturally would be first in authority in the absence of the first in authority. The contingency does not look to me to be one that would probably arise, or arise very often, at all events, and if the British Government is ready to accept it, I cannot see what we have to risk in that regard. For that matter, I do not see what they have; but if there should be any question in the matter, it would be from their point of view rather than from ours.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
There is another matter I wish to refer to. There are certain constitutional authorities, Mr. Curtiss, for instance, who are advocates of Imperial federation, who contend that the Dominion cannot have diplomatic representatives in foreign countries unless there is an Imperial Parliament to which those representatives are responsible, or unless there is complete independence. I do not say that Mr. Curtiss is right in that contention, but it may be that those who believe as Mr. Curtiss does will use this appointment of a Canadian representative as an argument for the creation of an Imperial Parliament. The question of constitutional relations between the various parts of the Empire will be discussed at a conference which it has been decided to hold, but which I believe has been postponed again until next year, and there sooner or later this question will be fully discussed. Can my right hon. friend give us the assurance that this appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington will not at all serve as an argument to strengthen the

position of Mr. Curtiss and those who believe as he does?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I saw in the newspaper this afternoon some comment on what was described as a tall order, but its tallness did not begin to compare with what my hon. friend puts up to me now. I cannot give him any assurance that the appointment of this ambassador will not be used as an argument for an Imperial Parliament or for anything else on earth.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
But would my right
hon. friend himself consider it as an argument for an Imperial Parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: My experience of controversy is, although I am not addicted to the habit myself, that controversialists will use almost anything as an argument for almost anything. I answer my hon. friend frankly; I do not think it would be an argument. Wonderful are the constitutional evolutions of the British Empire, and things that great authorities thought would be utterly impossible have turned out to be quite possible, and quite beneficent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It appears to me
that this proposal constitutes one of the gravest departures in constitutional affairs that we have seen in Canada within a generation. Although I allowed the vote to pass last year without saying a word upon it,
I have thought over it a great deal during the year, and I have been condemning myself that I did not on that occasion raise my voice in protest against the proposal.
I am here to-night to say that I agree almost entirely with the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Eielding) this afternoon as to the appointment of an ambassador to Washington.
I dissociate myself, however from that part of his address that referred to the recently proposed reciprocity agreement, which had no place whatever in the discussion so far as the constitutional question was concerned, and was simply introduced to show that Canada had exercised the rights of a free man to take up trade questions at Washington without let or hindrance from the British Government. Therefore, we have at present in our possession all the legitimate powers that a great overseas dominion could hope to have as a constituent part of the Empire. I consider that this is a very grave constitutional departure, and before it is embarked upon I think it should be debated on every hustings in every county in every province of Canada, so that the 
people of this country may be informed just what this step means and where it is going to lead.
I have listened with very careful attention to the addresses of hon. gentlemen who spoke this afternoon, but to my mind they avoided all the important constitutional issues that are bound up in this question. In the first place, Mr. Chairman, what right has the Dominion of Canada to appoint an ambassador that is not vested in every other overseas dominion of the Empire? Has Canada any constitutional right to appoint an ambassador that we do not allow South Africa, New Zealand, Australia, and all the other parts of the Empire to be partakers in? They have just as much right to apoint ambassadors to the United States or other countries as we have. Furthermore, to appoint an ambasador is to exercise the right of a sovereign power, and it is beggaring the question to say that the man whom it is intended to appoint will be a trade representative. The word used is "ambassador," and an ambassador to a foreign country can be sent only by a sovereign power, so far as we understand the constitutional prerogative. Never has the Dominion of Canada up to this date appointed an ambassador to the United States or any other country. Never has that right been exercised up to this time, and T have not heard that we have received any particular authority from Great Britain to embark upon so important a departure as this. As I view this question, it is another olfshoot of that evil genius, the League of Nations, which we had under discussion last night, and this whole thing has been forced upon us largely by that body. We have chosen to call ourselves a first class power, but we are not a first class power measured by the standards of the world. We may be a first class power insofar possibly as our resources and extent of territory are concerned; but no man can contend that Canada, in the essential sense of the word, is a first class nation; she is a first class power only as part of the British Empire.
The British Empire is a first class Empire, and it is quite good enough for us to remain in, retaining the contitutional status we have now. But to say that Canada is a first class power is to make a declaration that is not borne out by the facts.
A first class power must have very large and strong elements in its constitution, if it is to take its place on an equal footing among the great nations of the world;

and we have not the great essentials. A first class power must have a great army and navy, as well as population and resources. We have the resources, hut we have not the population, nor the army nor the navy; nor can it be contended for a moment that we are in a position to take up the full share of the white man's burden s which must be shouldered by a first class power. I was hoping that the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), had wilfully delayed the appointment of this ambassador for a year; but I am sorry to say to-night that he has rather indicated that such is noc the case, but that he is disposed to.name a man as soon as one properly qualified comes to light. Well, I think that there are plenty of proper men available, so far as that is concerned; but I doubt very much the wisdom of Canada embarking on such an enterprise as is proposed in the resolution. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), has properly said that $60,000 is quite an amount, but it is nothing to What we shall have to pay.
Further, I want to make this other point, that we have no more right to appoint an ambassador to the United States than we have the right to appoint one to France, or Germany, or Belgium, or Spain, or Russia, or any other country in the world. The same power is requisite to appoint an ambassador to the United States as to any of these countries. To say that there is more business carried on with the United States is immaterial. It is not a matter of business, or extent of business; it is a question whether or not sovereign rights are vested in Canada today to make the appointment. I contend that they are not, unless there is evidence to the contrary in the possession of the Government which they have not submitted to the House. I do sincerely hope that the Government will not embark on an enterprise that is going to get us into great difficulties. If we have an ambassador at Washington with equal powers with the British Ambassador, it is not far distant for any one to see that these two officials 'will come into conflict on certain questions. That is inevitable; it is as sure as the sun shines, that there will be questions on which they will not see eye to eye, because no two men can agree absolutely on every point. If that is the case, what will be the , situation if all the Dominions overseas appoint ambassadors to the United States and to all the other nations of the world? I say that this is only the beginning, because if we can exercise the power of appointing one ambassador we can appoint ten or twenty. But, Mr. Chairman, we must have all the constituent qualities of a great nation in order to be able to do that. It is a very unwise step to do anything of the kind and I trust it will not be undertaken without the most serious consideration on the part of the Prime Minister and the cabinet surrounding him.
I have not the means of knowing whether the Cabinet is unanimous on this question, but I for one, from the moment it was mooted, have been absolutely against it. As a rule, I cannot agree with the member for Shelburne and Queen's, but I must say that he has interpreted my view on this question perfectly. To my mind, this is so important a question, and the consequences to which it will lead are of so far-reaching a character, that the people of Canada should be taken into the confidence of the House, and of the Government, and the whole subject should be thoroughly debated in the country so that we may see clearly the significance, that we are at the parting of the ways. I interpret this proposal as a distinct announcement to the world that Canada is going to embark upon nationhood herself, regardless of the old motherland. I cannot interpret it in any other way, and the idle suggestion that there is nothing to fear, that all is plain sailing, does not commend itself to my judgment at all. I say it is the most serious question that could be considered, and it should be taken into earnest consideration by every member of the House and by every citizen who desires to have permen-ent British connection such as we have always had.
Now, what has arisen that has caused us to be dissatisfied with prevailing conditions? Are there any outstanding and burning questions between the United States and Canada to-day that cannot be settled through the ordinary diplomatic channels as provided by the British Government? I cannot see where there are. If it is a matter of appointing trade agents, then let us have trade agents; I am in favour of that, and I should like to have not only one but twenty or thirty trade agents appointed to the United States in all the principal cities. I have never used the phrase "no truck nor trade with the Yankees." I do not use it now, and I think that we ought to have consular agents over there. But a consular agent is a very different person from an ambassador who stands in the other country clothed with the right to speak for all of the people whom he rep re-

sents, and in whose hands are the issues of peace and war. Surely It cannot be contended for a moment that Canada possesses the right at the present time to appoint an official vested with this authority. It cannot be contended that this is our right merely because we signed a document in the League of Nations dissociating ourselves from the other members of the British Empire. The signing of that document does not constitute us a first-class power, and make us a great nation ready to take upon ourselves the full responsibilities of a first-class power. To be a first-class nation we must be ready to spend hundreds of millions of dollars and to show that we can bear our share of the white man's burden in this and in every other part of the world. Canada's position in the League of Nations does not warrant her in separating herself from the Empire as an individual entity, a power with the right to appoint ambassadors in every country. If Canada can do this, then all the overseas dominions can do the same; because it cannot be successfully contended that their rights are not exactly the same as ours. The only thing that can be said is that they do not transact as much business with the United States as we do, but that is not the question at all. The question is a constitutional one: Have we, as part of the British Empire, the right to step out regardless of what the views of the Empire are? I cannot see for a moment that that position can be justified.
Furthermore, if we appoint an ambassador to the United States, the question arises: are they going to appoint an ambassador to Canada? The one, of course, follows as a natural consequence of the other. We have only American consuls in the Dominion of Canada to-day. Surely we are not going to appoint an ambassador to the United States and have them reciprocate merely with consular agents. And every other country to which we might send an ambassador should be under the obligation to have an ambassador in Ottawa. Now, Mr. Chairman, I cannot contemplate that the Government intends to embark on so vast a scheme. Every argument that can be used in connection with this one appointment could with equal force be advanced as regards any other similar appointment that might be proposed for an ambassador in France or any other country in the world. I cannot possibly conceive how the Government can stand up and justify an appointment that will have such far-reaching consequences, without

practically taking a plebiscite of the people of Canada on the question whether or not they are dissatisfied with British connection and desire to embark upon a policy that will, with absolute certainty, lead us away from the Motherland, and land us goodness knows where in a display which we cannot back up by a delivery of the goods. We have not got the goods to deliver. I have great respect for the resources and capacity of the Dominion of Canada, but if our railways have been built fifty years too early, it does not follow that we should appoint ambassadors fifty or a hundred years ahead of time, and that is practically what this amounts to. We are in no position to-day to say that we are a first-class, power with the rights and liberties to appoint ambassadors. If the appointment of a Canadian ambassador has been agreed to, where is the document from the Home Government authorizing it? We have not heard a word on that head up to date. We have not heard a single word showing that the British Government have expressed their consent to the appointment of an ambassador of this kind, which evidently is the thin end of the wedge of separation. If such a document is in the possession of this Government I think it is time to produce it so that we may have all the facts before us. If we have decided to embark on a policy that is going to lead ultimately to separation, why let us know that we may go into it with our eyes open; but do not let us embark upon a policy that is going to lead us into a vast amount of entanglement and difficulty when we have not the wherewithal to back that policy up and to show that we are able to maintain the position that we claim to occupy-that of a great and first-class nation in the world.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
While I do not agree
with everything the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has said, I am strongly of the opinion that the item of $60,000 for Canadian representation in the United States is merely a subterfuge to hide something greater. I believe that the House is entitled to be taken into the confidence of the Government upon this item. In view of the fact that the House some time ago abolished titles, or attempted to as far as Canada could operate, this seems to be rather a high-sounding symbol of something similar in the upper strata of Canadian public life. It does not savour of the democratic very much. If the item to provide for the appointment of a Canadian

ambassador it should be twice $60,000, because, if Canada were sending an ambassador to the great nation to the south, the money advanced to him would have to comport with the dignity of his office. He could not possibly maintain an establishment suitable to the magnitude and importance of this country at the capitol of the United States on any paltry $60,000; and he would have to pay his staff in addition to supporting himself and his household. On the other hand, if it is for the purpose of establishing a centre round which will gravitate and operate an organization which will be equal to the consular system of the United States for trade purposes I would hold up both hands for it. When the Estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were before the House I took occasion to point out, in a very meagre way, the situation as it appeared to me with regard to the great need for Canada at the present time. The need is not to give some man a place for diplomatic purposes; the need is to appoint many men for the benefit of this country in order to enlarge the trade of Canada in every market of the world where it can be enlarged to good purpose and to good effect. We have a sort of system of trade agencies throughout the far off nations of the world, yet although we have 110,000,000 people adjacent to us, and have trade agents in every litle nation and at every little point throughout Europe and Asia, we have not a consular agent or a trade agent, or a trade representative in this 110,000,000 market at our door.
We sold something like $552,000,000 worth of products to the United States last year and we did so without trying. It is a mathematical proposition as to how much we could sell if we were to try. The United States sold us $2 worth of their products for every $1 worth we sold them. How do they do it? They have a most remarkable establishment in this country of consular agents. A people of 110,000,000 think enough of this country of 9,000,000 to send into Canada 92 consuls, vice-consuls and consular agents entirely for the purposes of trade. Upon that proportion of commercial activity, feeling that there is a field for United States trade in this country, they sent into Canada 92 active, trained, competent businesslike trade agents to pick up what trade they could get for themselves. We sent not one man to the United States or spent even a dollar for that purpose. These 92 agents that came to Canada did not come at the expense of the
United States. They sit down here and do the business and they make it pay them. The fees they collected for the viseing of invoices overpays the cost of these 92 agents by very large sums.
Let me explain to those who may not have looked into the matter just how they do it. The principle of viseing invoices is applied by many countries in the world who send out trade agents to other nations. Mexico and Equador charge 3 per cent upon all invoices upon their country; Peru, Bolivia and Guatemala, 2 per cent; France, $2.40 per invoice; Japan, $4; Italy, $3.89; Spain, $12; Norway, $2.70. On that principle the American consular service sits down in Canada and in the last eight years it collected $2,595,326.95 as against a total expenditure of $1,630,823.80. It is made to pay, as the figures show a profit of nearly a million dollars during the years 1913 to 1920 inclusive, out of the pockets of the Canadian people. Now let me put this proposition to the House: If Canada, without trying and without even one consular agent, has a natural trade with the United States running into $552,000,000 a year, what would her trade be if we placed in the United States sixty, seventy or a hundred consular agents? There is probably a false impression as to the kind of goods that pass between the two countries. I would like to lay before the House these facts-that in the twelve months ending March 31, 1920, Canada sold to the United States a considerable quantity of manufactured goods. The percentages, as compiled by the Dominion statistician, are as follows:
Raw Materials, 42.8 per cent.

I certainly do not
want to interrupt the trend of the argument of my hon. friend and I think he should be allowed to complete that argument, but I must remind him, and remind the committee, that discussion of the point as to trade commissions, or trade agents, or consular agents in the United States, or any other country is certainly not in order under this item. We have already had a discussion on that subject under item 358 of the Estimates of the Trade and Commerce Department. As I said before, while I do not want to interrupt the hon. member in the middle of his argument, I hope it will not be extended.
