subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I always like to bow to the ruling of the Chair, but I take up the Estimates at page 63 and find " Canadian Representation in the United States " without a definite classification of the repre-

sentatiou, and when the Government has not really been too outspoken as to whether or not they ever would fill the ambassadorial post, I thought as a member I was entitled to object to the item, upon the ground that I did not think that was as good a kind of representation by itself as I would advocate. That is the purpose of my argument, and I think I ought to be allowed to follow it up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The Chair cannot very well reverse the ruling. The hon. member should not consider it unfair when it was stated that he should be allowed to finish the argument which he had undertaken. His objection to the ruling would be perfectly well taken if there was no other item in the Estimates covering the particular object which the hon. member is now discussing; but that is specifically covered by the item " Trade Commissioners and Commercial agents." This applies to all countries.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That item has been
passed, as I understand?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, it has been
passed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: And there is no possibility of discussing it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: There is a well known rule that the same question cannot be debated twice.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I will follow the ruling of the Chair and take an opportunity on the Budget as my remarks will be somewhat prolonged to give my views on Canadian representation in the United States either alone or in connection with a Canadian ambassador.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Before I
make the few remarks I intend to offer, may I ask my right hon. friend whether the Government has changed its mind in the matter of giving this House any correspondence which will throw light on the negotiations between the British Government, the Government of the United States and the Canadian Government with reference to the particular appointment which we have been discussing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The Government has not changed its mind. I have had the matter carefully looked into by the legal adviser of the External Affairs Department. Inasmuch as the negotiations, or whatever you may care to describe them, took place not only with the United States particularly but also with Great Britain,

it was a tripartite correspondence, and it is not the practice of governments to make public correspondence leading to an agreement or to a covenant; nor have we the right to make it public, because it affects the United States. And it would be just the same if they made it public, which they have not done. I have had the advantage of discussing the subject with the gentleman to whom I refer, and he is very clear -and I am very clear after that discussion-that the Government would have no right to make the correspondence public. Furthermore, there would be nothing gained by doing so as everything is disclosed in the conclusions arrived at and which constitute the consensus ad idem between the parties. They have been made public, but I think it would be better for me to read them anew. This is the statement made to the House on May 10, 1920, which embodies the arrangement:
As a result of recent discussions an arrangement has been concluded between the British and Canadian Governments to provide more complete representation at Washington of Canadian interests than has hitherto existed Accordingly, it has been agreed that His Majesty, on advice of his Canadian ministers, shall appoint a Minister Plenipotentiary who will have charge of Canadian affairs and will at all times be the ordinary channel of communication with the United States Government in matters of purely Canadian concern, acting upon instructions from and reporting direct to the Canadian Government, In the absence of the Ambassador the Canadian minister will take charge of the whole Embassy and of the representation of Imperial as well as Canadian interests. He will be accredited by His Majesty to the President with the necessary powers for the purpose.
This new arrangement will not denote any departure either on the part of the British Government or of the Canadian Government from the principle of the diplomatic unity of the British Empire.
The need for this important step has been fully realized by -both Governments for some time. For a good many years there has been direct communication between Washington and Ottawa, but the constantly increasing importance of Canadian interests in the United States has made it apparent that Canada should be represented there in some distinctive manner, for this would doubtless tend to expedite negotiations, and naturally first-hand acquaintance with Canadian conditions would promote good understanding. In view of the peculiarly close relations that have always existed between the people of Canada and those of the United States, it is confidently expected as well that this new step will have the very desirable result of maintaining and strengthening the friendly relations and co-operation between the British Empire and the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am not sure that I caught my right hon. friend correctly. Did he say that I had discussed this matter with him?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: No. I consulted the legal adviser of the External Affairs Department, Mr. Christie, with regard to the right of the Government to bring down the correspondence leading to the conclusions between the three governments. His advice is that it is never done, and certainly we could not do it in this instance.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Was not the correspondence betwen the United States Government and the Government of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: It was a tripartite correspondence, and for that reason the United States Government had to be consulted. We do sometimes bring down correspondence between the Home Government and ourselves; but Mr. Christie has looked through this correspondence, and his conclusion is that there is nothing that we have a right to bring down, and, further, that there would be no advantage in doing so because the conclusions arrived at are all set out in this statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I certainly would not like to pit my own opinion against that of the legal expert of the Department of External Affairs, especially as my right hon. friend is prepared to accept that opinion, but I do think it is an extraordinary thing when this country is about to take a departure in the way of appointing a minister plenipotentiary to another country that not a single document of record is placed upon the table of the House which will establish for all time, beyond any possibility of misunderstanding, the exact terms of the arrangement between, first, the Government of Canada and the Government of Great Britain; second, the Government of Great Britain and the Government of the United States, and third, the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The statement which I have just read is an exact statement of the understanding.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: My right hon. friend gives us a statement which he says is the exact statement of the understanding. Of course, we will accept his word for that. On the other hand, it is quite possible we may find later on that either the Government of the United States or the British Government might not wholly agree with my right hon. friend's view as to this being an exact statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My right hon. friend on my left (Mr. Rowell) advises me that
this precise statement was also read in the British House on the same day that it was read here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Has it been
read in Congress?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I could not say as to that. The United States was simply consulted as to the arrangement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I think unless we have some assurance from the United States that this statement is satisfactory to them, we are proceeding in the dark, at least to that extent. I certainly think this Parliament should have before it in the form of some permanent record communications from the Governments of Great Britain and of the United States that this statement does represent what they are agreed upon as the arrangement to be entered into. But apart from that, taking this statement on its face value, it throws very little light upon the subject, for it tells us very little of what the real powers and functions of this new particular plenipotentiary are to be. We have had him described in this House to-day as an ambassador. I think the term used in the statement is "Minister Plenipotentiary," which is comprehensive enough. At least we ought to have something which will set forth in precise detail what are the rights, duties and functions of this particular appointee.
I do not ask my right hon. friend to take simply my own expression of opinion as to this being the correct attitude. I think it is the public opinion of this country. The press, so far as it has given expression to its views on this important subject, has rather strongly supported the position which we on this side of the House took last year, that more detailed and accurate information should be furnished before Parliament went ahead and sanctioned this appointment. It is interesting to-night to observe that hon. members on the other side of the House are concurring entirely with the view which we of the Opposition took last year when the statement which my right hon. friend has just read was presented to the House. My hon. friend from Perth will recall that at that time we on this side moved the following resolution which, had it been carried, might have avoided a good deal of the discussion which we are having to-night:
The (House desires to record its opinion that before any arrangement respecting the permanent representation of Canada at Washington is consummated, the House should be fully

informed concerning the negotiations between the Canadian, Imperial and United States Governments, and all correspondence and Orders in Council on the subject should be submitted to the House.
Now that is precisely what my hon. friend from Perth has been saying to-night we should have, and is precisely what the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) has been saying we should have. Yet when I look at the division list I find that at the last session my hon. friend from Perth voted against that resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I was not permitted to finish my remarks; therefore you do not know exactly where I am.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Well, we shall be glad to hear my hon. friend's further explanation. However, our position to-night is exactly what it was at that time in regard to an understanding of the authority and rights of this particular official.
I said a moment ago that I thought I was expresing the views of the press of this country. I would like to give just one quotation, one that my right hon. friend will recognize as deserving of careful consideration on the part of this committee. No Canadian journal that I am aware of has given more thoughtful consideration to this matter of the appointment of a minister to Washington than the Winnipeg Free Press. The Free Press has published several articles on this subject. I shall read only one, but I think it will be sufficient to show that every question raised in committee this afternoon is, in the opinion of this journal, a proper and correct question to raise. Moreover, while some exception was taken to the views expressed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, I find that exactly the same questions raised by him are mentioned by this journal as being those on which Parliament should be more fully informed before we finally determine what should be done; among those questions was included that of whether this minister would have the right to sign his own name or whether the British ambassador would still have to sign. The editorial from which I shall quote will be found in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 12, 1920, when this subject was up last year. It reads:
The ap-poinfcment of a Canadian Minister Plenipotentiary at Washington is an interesting innovation about which it will be possible to comment intelligently when more information is available than was supplied in the very guarded statement read in the House of Commons on Monday by Sir George Poster.
 '
This is the same statement that my right hon. friend has read to the House to-night. I shall skip the paragraph that follows and go on:
It is intimated that our Canadian minister will deal with all matters arising between Canada and the United States which are exclusively Canadian in character; the Imperial ambassador will participate in the negotiations only when Imperial interests are involved. Very well; but what 'happens if a disagreement should arise-which might easily happen- between the Canadian minister and the British ambassador as to whether a question is, or is not, exclusively Canadian? Even in. the exclusively Canadian matters about which there is no dispute, will the Canadian minister carry negotiations through to the end ; or will it be necessary, in the final resort, to Call in the British minister to do the actual signing?
Now, that is the point which was raised by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's this afternoon. My hon. friend from Durham took exception to 9 p.m. his remarks. He said the member for Shelburne and Queen's took the position that we could do nothing except through the British Foreign Office; that we had to have action by the British Foreign Office. That is what the hon. member said in representing the view expressed by the member for Shelburne and Queen's.
' Mr. ROWELL: I did not say he said that^ exactly; he did not say that exactly. I said I took that to he the logical deduction from the argument he presented.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Well, if that is the logical deduction it is evidently a question that is very much in the mind of a journal which takes an independent attitude in regard to this subject and wants to get the light which this Parliament ought to get upon it. The question that the Winnipeg Free Press puts is:
Will it be necessary, in the final resort, to call in the British Minister to do the actual signing? Our representative is to be known as a minister. Will he be accepted as a minister by the . State Department at Washington?
We have had no assurance upon that point. We ought to know whether he will or will not.
Will he be a member of the diplomatic corps, having all the rights, powers, immunities and privileges enjoyed by the ministers of all other countries represented at Washington? Will he be the equal in diplomatic status of, let us say, the minister from Venezuela? Or will his position at Washington be actually undefined with a mere courtesy status? Parliament and the country will peed conclusive answer to these and similar questions; and not until this information is supplied will it be possible to say whether this is a step forward or backward.
Now, if my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's had used that language this

afternoon, the member for Durham would have called him antiquated and referred to him as still holding to the point of view that we have but a colonial status. I put the question to my hon. friend as coming from one of the thoughtful journals of this country and as evidence of the need for precisely the kind of information that is requested from this side to-day. The article continues:
It is asserted in certain quarters that this marks an enlargement of Canadian powers and that it is another step forward on the road to nationhood. ,The Government at Ottawa no doubt believes that this will be the effect of the innovation. But we regard with some trepidation formal arrangements entered into three years after the adoption of a declared policy of equality of status between all the British nations by which it is possible that Canada may accept, ratify, and confirm a status of admitted diplomatic inferiority, formally putting her name to documents that confirm this subordination. If the Canadian minister at Washington is only a camouflaged chief clerk or a commissioner it would be better to have no minister there.
If his position there is by courtesy, if Canada cannot endow her representative with all the powers which other ministers enjoy, then Canada should send no one to Washington until she can vest him with the true prerogatives of office.
Information upon these extremely important points is lacking; until it is forthcoming any conclusive judgment upon the wisdom or otherwise of the Government's action is not possible. But the matter is of great importance and Parliament should regard it as one of its prime duties to see that the matter is fully discussed [DOT] from all angles and in the light of full knowledge.
I ask the pardon of the committee for taking up so much time in the reading of a long extract, but every point raised in that editorial is pertinent to the discussion, and I think the ministry should answer the questions here raised before they ask us to vote, without this knowledge, some $60,000 to establish a position whereby the country will incur vast obligations as a beginning and incur still greater obligations as time goes on.
I should also point out that this is the first departure, or one of the first, that this country has made in what we may call its permanent representation in the matter of external diplomatic relations. To begin our foreign diplomacy by secrecy with respect to the precise nature of understandings arrived at is unfortunate, to say the least, in so far-reaching a departure.
A considerable part of the discussion this afternoon turned on the question of Canada's status. In view of some remarks made from this side it might be inferred without reflection that we held the view
that Canada's status had not changed in many years; that Canada was still in the position which she occupied quite a number of years ago. Well, the whole question of Canada's status in matters of this kind turns upon whether we are thinking and speaking of the spirit or of the letter of the constitution. If we are speaking of the letter of the constitution, or, as my hon. friend for Durham has put it, the legal rights that we have under the constitution, there can be no doubt whatever of the correctness of the view expressed by the member for Shelburne and Queen's this afternoon, that Canada is not a nation in the sense in which that term is used when the full rights of nationhood or, in other words, the rights of a sovereign nation are implied. On the other hand, if it is to the spirit of the constitution that we are looking, or, as my hon. friend for Durham said this afternoon, if we approach the matter from the standpoint of constitutional authority, then I agree entirely with him that we have the status of a nation. It is not a status that we have acquired recently; it is a status that we have had for a number of years, but which has become more clearly defined in recent years, especially during the period of the war. It was mentioned to-day that inasmuch as we could not amend the constitution of Canada without the British Parliament amending it, that was a sign of inferiority. In this connection may I say that New Zealand and Australia have each the right to amend their constitutions without any appeal to the British Government, they are self-governing Dominions. I have no doubt that if we asked the British Government to give us the same right to amend our constitution without referring the matter to Great Britain, we would be given that right. It is a matter, so far as I can see, simply of constitutional development as to whether we take a further step which may give us still more in the way of the status of a nation to outward appearances without prejudicing the unity of the Empire as a whole.	>
There is a matter which, perhaps, the committee will pardon me referring to. I mention it simply because I think it has some value in a discussion of this kind relative to Canada's status and the right of Canada's ministers to act in the name of the Sovereign. I gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell) that he contended that the King of England was also King of Canada,

and that a Canadian minister should have the same right and authority to make a treaty in the name of the King as any minister of the British Government. Let me say that I agree entirely with the point of view he has expressed, and my purpose in mentioning the incident to which I shall refer is to indicate that the British Government has, to my certain knowledge, held that view for some time past. In 1908,1 had the privilege of being appointed one of the delegates, the representative of this country, to the International Conference on the opium traffic which met at Shanghai, China. Before I left for that conference, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was Prime Minister at that time, asked me to proceed to China by way of England and, while in England, to see the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and ascertain whether it would be agreeable to the Government of Great Britain as it was the wish of our Government to have a treaty entered into between the Chinese Government and the Government of Canada with respect to immigration to this country from China, to have an arrangement made with' China similar to the arrangement which we had with Japan. The view which Sir Wilfrid Laurier held at that time was that the question of immigration could be better regulated by means of a treaty arrangement between the two countries than by the form which it both then and still takes of a head tax upon the Chinese. Sir Wilfrid Laurier asked me to ascertain from the Foreign Secretary of Great Britain what view Great Britain would take as regards a treaty on that subject being made with the Chinese Government. The then Secretary Sir Edward Grey, at present Lord Grey, took the position at the time that a minister of the Crown in Canada had as much right to act in the name of the Sovereign as any minister of the Crown in Great Britain, and that a minister of the Crown in Canada might receive from the King in England the same authority to act in the negotiating and the signing of a treaty as could be given to any British minister. I mention this, because I think it is important that the committee should know the view held at a period as early as 1908 by the then Secretary for Foreign Affairs in Great Britain.
As to the question of the wisdom of having a representative of Canada at Washington, I for one feel that it is wholly in the interest of this country to have someone represent us in an official position at

Washington, so that it may be possible for the Government of Canada to be informed from day to day from an authoritative source in regard to matters of concern to the two countries, and ministers of the Crown in Canada acquaint Secretaries of State in the United States with and learn from them their views on matters, of mutual concern. We have many questions of trade, immigration, industrial relations, international relations, on which we have much in common, and as regards which there are many considerations which both governments should take into account. While some years ago, perhaps, a step of the kind was unnecessary, I think that today, as our population grows, as the problems of the British Empire grow, as British ministers have more and more to attend to in connection with their own affairs, it is wholly in the interest of our country to have its own representation.
There is such a thing however as going from one extreme to the other. At the one extreme you have the thought that we should have no representative, but be represented exclusively by the British Embassy. At the other extreme is the idea put forward in the statement which my right hon. friend has just read, that a Canadian minister should take over the Embassy and be in charge of Imperial policy when the British ambassador is not present. I think the last proposal is a great mistake, and I do not think this Parliament should authorise any representative from Canada to assume complete control of the British Embassy at Washington. Once a step of that kind is taken, it may lead to all kinds of complications, embarrassments, and misunderstandings. The best way to preserve friendship and unity between all parts of the British Empire is to avoid, as far as possible, any possibility of complications and misunderstandings. I cannot but fear that if a Canadian minister should, while in charge of the British Embassy, perform any act which might be displeasing to the British authorities one way or another, relations between Canada and Great Bratain might become very strained as a consequence. Moreover, there are questions in regard to which British interests may be one thing and Canadian interests another. In such a circumstance, it is putting a representative of Canada in a most unfair position to have him given charge of the British Embassy as well as charge of Canadian affairs. Moreover, I think it is a fatal position from the point of view of respon-

sibility. No man can serve two masters. If a minister is representing Canada and representing Great Britain, he must be responsible to the two. It is useless to say that the possibility may never arise; it is almost inevitable that sooner or later it will arise. I hope my hon. friends, in attempting to carry out this policy of appointing a minister to Washington, will, at least, reconsider that particular aspect, and let us begin in a modest and natural way. Let us follow the line of evolution and for the time being put our minister in charge only of Canadian affairs. Later on, after he has had considerable experience and we see how the first step works out, we can consider the further step.
In conclusion, I wish to say to my right hon. friend that I was somewhat amused at the reason he gave for no appointment being made to this high office, that there was not a good man available. That is surely very uncomplimentary to the hundred and fifty odd gentlemen whom my right hon. friend has as followers behind him. I think my right hon. friend will find that they are all available if he asks them. It is for him to say whether they are good or not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt). Once or twice during his remarks, I was almost persuaded that we had severed ourselves from the British Empire. The conclusions at which he arrives would, perhaps, be correct if they had been well founded, but the difficulty with his whole argument was that it was based absolutely on false premises. I see nothing about an appointment by the Dominion of Canada of an ambassador to the United States, nor have I heard it suggested anywhere that an ambassador be appointed by this country, nor does the item in the appropriation in the least degree suggest that. I agree thoroughly with the utterances of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in so far as he suggests that we should have a higher standard of representation by this country in the United States than merely trade agents. We will assume, for the sake of argument, that some serious question other than one of mere trade arises between these two countries and we have only men appoint' ed as trade agents in the city of New York and other cities in that great Republic. Would they have any authority to deal concerning that question with the
Government of the United States? One must realise at once that a man who is appointed simply in the capacity of a trade agent has the duties merely of a trade agent, to look after the commercial interest of our country. The great difficulty in my hon. friend's mind seems to be that if we appoint a representative in this official capacity, we are, by so doing, difting from the Motherland and weakening the ties which exist between Great Britain and the Dominion of Canada. We, however, have that offset by the argument of the hon. leader of the Opposition. His argument is that this arrangement will draw us closer to the British Empire, while the argument of my hon. friend is that it will drive us away from the British Empire. Which of these two arguments is correct? I believe that the argument which has been submitted by the hon. leader of the Opposition is the correct one. I believe that instead of having a tendency to separate ourselves from the British Empire by the appointment of such an official, under the arrangement which has been arrived at between the United States, Great Britain and Canada, we shall be drawing ourselves closer to Great Britain than we ai-e at the present time. We must arrive at this conclusion from the mere fact of the memorandum which has been read to the House by the Prime Minister to-night. If this step were a move towards separation, does my hon. friend for one moment suppose that this House could convince itself that Great Britain would appoint our ambassador to take over the duties of the British ambassador in his absence? I say that this step will simply draw us closer to the British Empire, and if my hon. friend has any doubts along that line he should remove them and retract his words, and support the appropriation which is asked for to-night.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Not very much.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "not very much." Would the hon. gentleman severe his relationship with any individual and then expect to have that individual appointed to a position of trust and responsibility on his behalf? This official is being appointed to a position of responsibility because Great Britain realizes the closeness of the ties between the Dominion of Canada and herself. She reposes such confidence in this country, that she has seen fit to extend it to the point where she would allow the Dominion of Canada by reason of closer relationship to participate



with the embassy in Washington in the administration of her foreign affairs in the United States. I have no doubt that my hon. friend from Perth and my hon. friend from Brantford are the very gentlemen who in times past have protested against the injustices which this country has suffered by reason of the manner in which matters affecting Canada have been handled by the British ambassador at Washington. We have had our disputes about the boundary line between the United States and Canada from the East right straight through to the West, and complaints have repeatedly been made that the British ambassador in Washington has sacrificed the interests of Canada to the United States. If we have a representative at Washington in close touch with the British ambassador, as is proposed, we will have the opportunity of presenting our case directly through the British ambassador at the time the negotiations are being carried on, or of having our own representative carry on the negotiations on behalf of the Dominion. I believe that if that system had prevailed in the past, this country would have been the gainer by many hundreds of thousands of acres, if not square miles, of territory which have been lost to us as the result of the negotiations being carried on simply by the British ambassador without Canada having a representative at Washington.
So far from the performance of these acts being an indication of separation from the Mother Land, surely my hon. friend (Mr. Coclcshutt) realizes that the constitutional development of this country, like the constitutional development of Great Britain or any other country has been a matter of slow progress. In the early years of the Dominion of Canada, it was' unthought of that any minister in this country should even negotiate trade treaties much less have any participation whatever in their execution. Great Britain, however, has seen fit to delegate additional power to this country so that now our ministers are able to negotiate these treaties and execute them along with the plenipotentiaries of Great Britain. Can it be argued that because that power has been granted to us, there is any separation by the Dominion of Canada from the Empire? No, it means that our status has changed, and as the leader of the Opposition says, we must look at this matter not in a strict technical sense, but in the spirit of the constitution. We are becoming a greater country, we are becoming more indepenfMr. Tweedie.]
dent, but we are not separating ourselves from the Mother Land. I would be the last man in this House to support the Government in doing anything which would in the slightest degree lessen the close relations which we have with the Mother Land, and this I understand to be the view of the Prime Minister. I have very great pleasure in supporting this appropriation as set forth in the Estimates, for the reasons I have given and I believe it is the duty of every man in this House to support it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have had a very interesting discussion extending now for some hours, and I doubt if there is anything new by way of argument that I can add to the debate. I want at once to express my personal appreciation of the statement given to the House this afternoon by my right hon. friend from King's (Sir Robert Borden). This question of Canada's position in the world and of our taking on new responsibilities is one that is receiving a great deal of attention to-day throughout the country. Many are studying it who a few years ago gave no attention to it whatever, and I am very certain that the information submitted to the House this afternoon by my right hon. friend from King's will be of very great assistance to students of this question in familiarizing themselves with our development along constitutional lines.
Let me say at once that I find myself in very general agreement indeed, not only with the sentiments expressed by my right hon. friend from King's, but with the argument made by my right hon. friend from Durham and with much that was said by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I cannot take the gloomy view of this step, by which it is proposed to send a minister to Washington, that my hon. friend from Brantford does. I think if we study the history of this country we shall find this one fact outstanding, that every time we have had an extension of the powers of self-government in Canada, every time we have had an addition to our autonomy as a people, the result has been a closer and a better understanding with the Mother Country. That has invariably been the case. I know that in 1840, when the Act of Union was passed, whereby a large measure of self-government was given to the provinces of Canada, there were those at that time who saw in that step a breaking of the links that bound the inhabitants of this country to the

Mother Land. Again, in 1867, when the great confederation of the provinces took place and when our powers of self-government were again greatly enlarged, there were also those who saw in that another snapping of the ties that bound us to Great Britain. But has that been the result? I believe that if my hon. friend from Brantford had been living and had been in active political life in those days, he would have taken the position then in respect to the enlargement of Canadian autonomy that he has taken to-day in respect to the proposal we are now considering. I say that in all sincerity, because I wish to bear this testimony to my hon. friend's sincerity, that in my judgment, there is not a member of this House who speaks with greater honesty of conviction than does my hon. friend from Brantford.
The vote we have under consideration at the present time is an important one, and I am glad to support it. I shall not traverse the ground that has already been covered by those who have preceded me in this debate, but I might emphasize this: our close relationship with the United States, the immense volume of business we do with that country, the great extent of our boundary line contiguous to that country, the fact that we speak a common language, the fact that we are daily mingling with each other- these considerations, Mr. Speaker, place our relationship with that country on a different plane from our relationship with other countries in the world. It is quite conceivable that the interests of Canada, touching so closely and intimately as they do the life of the United States, not from any lack of goodwill, but from pressure of other business may not receive that careful consideration from the British ambassador at Washington, which they should receive. I think my right hon. friend from King's (Sir Robert Borden), this afternoon stated that Lord Bryce had on one occasion borne testimony to the fact that more than half of the business he had to do with the Government at Washington was Canadian business; and I feel certain that this business can be much better looked after if we have our own minister plenipotentiary at Washington. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt), in his remarks this evening, said that the British Government had given no warrant for this appointment. I think the statement made a little earlier in this debate by the Prime Minister-I sent for it in order that I might read it myselfcovers that point very well. The arrangements leading up to the appointment of a Canadian minister plenipotentiary were taken up with the British Government, and the present position in the matter is in entire accord with the views of the British Government and has their approval.
I desire to refer to another point raised by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in respect of which I am inclined to agree with him. The matter was brought up in the House at the last session, that exchanges of communications which had taken place, leading up to the announcement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on May 10, 1920, should be placed before this Parliament and this country. Now, I have no use for secret diplomacy, but at the same time I recognize that it is quite possible that our Government might be acting improperly if they divulged these communications without the consent, of the British Government and the Government at Washington or at any rate without first acquainting these governments of their intention to do so. However, I would offer the suggestion to my right hon. friend who leads the Government, that he might very well inquire of the British Government, and of the Government at Washington, whether or not there is any objection to making public any communications that have been exchanged leading up to this understanding; and if the way is clear for giving this information to the Canadian people, if there is no good and valid reason why it should not be disclosed, then I am entirely in accord with the leader of the Opposition in his view that it should be submitted to Parliament and to the country.
I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that the step which is about to be taken will lead to good results, but I am inclined to criticise the Government for their failure, so far, to make this appointment. I am bound to say that in my opinion the Prime Minister did not advance a very good reason this evening when he said that no one competent for the position had so far been found. I would suggest to him that he look about him. There are plenty of able men in Canada who can fill the position, and I am sure my right hon. friend, with his ability and his knowledge of men, can quickly and readily find some one capable of taking the appointment, if he sets himself seriously to the task. I should like some information from the Government as to how soon they expect this appointment to be made, and whether they are working

assiduously in an effort to have the position filled. I know that this is a matter of importance to this country, especially at this time. Now that we are in a period of reconstruction after war, when international business is being largely rearranged, the time has certainly arrived when this matter should receive prompt consideration at the hands of the Government, and this appointment should be made without further delay.

speechtext:
As one of the representatives from the middle-western part of Canada, I should like to say a few words on this very interesting question which is now before the House. I think that the hon. member who has just concluded (Mr. Crerar) has expressed the views of Western Canada on this question, and I believe also that the House owes a debt of gratitude to the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) who to-day gave us a chronological history of the development of the question in Canada.
I desire to refer briefly to the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I do so very hesitatingly, because I hold that hon. gentleman in very high esteem and appreciate the difficulty that confronts a younger member who attempts to criticise the remarks of one who has had such a wide experience in the political life of this country as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. I usually listen to him with very great interest and deep respect, but there is one question upon which I have heard him speak on several occasions in this House in regard to which, it seems to me, he does not show that elasticity of mind and that progressiveness of thought which he generally displays on public questions. I refer now to the question of Canada's status, a question which more or less comes within the scope of the subject now before the House. For example, in his speech this afternoon he expressed himself in a manner that rather suggested to my mind that he was almost proud of the fact that Canadian representatives to-day cannot complete treaties on behalf of Canada. He also went on to say that practically we are a colony, and he finished a few moments later by saying that so far as he was concerned he wanted no change in our present condition. I do not think I am misquoting the hon. gentleman; certainly, if I do so it is altogether unintentional. That was my conclusion, [Ur. Crerar.]
at any rate, from the remarks he made, and I think I am stating his position fairly.
Well, Sir, I do not believe that if Canada were really a colony to-day her people would be satisfied that she should remain in that position. Personally, I do not agree that we are, to all intents and purposes, only a colony. I believe that we have progressed probably fifty years beyond the colonial stage. The hon. gentleman proceeded to say that we should be better represented by a minister in Ottawa who could travel from Ottawa to Washington on various occasions, than we should be if we had a representative, who kept in touch with Canadian affairs, residing at Washington. I have been wondering why it would be easier for a minister to travel from Ottawa to Washington and back again, than it would be for a representative at Washington to travel to Ottawa, to consult with the ministers' here, and then back to Washington.
I happened to-day to run across a message sent in 1907 by the Prime Minister of Great Britain to the Prime Minister of New Zealand, when that colony assumed the status of a Dominion. He said:
To-day your island home attains the prouder title of "Dominion."
I believe that the Prime Minister of Great Britain, in sending that message virtually admitted that we also had gone a long distance past the colonial stage and, Sir, I noticed in this morning's Citizen a quotation from Mr. Hughes, the Prime Minister of Australia, than whom, I think, no one will claim to be a more loyal British subject, and he does not agree with the view of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, or of those who take the position that we are. practically in the status we previously held, and that we must remain so. Mr. Hughes, in this morning's Citizen, is quoted at some length, and among other things he says:
We in the Australian Commonwealth now call ourselves a nation. So we are. But in the same breath we declare ourselves part of the British Empire. These apparently inconsistent declarations combine at once our history and our circumstance.
I believe, Sir, that that shows that the Prime Minister of Australia, a loyal Britisher, a man who was born in the British isles, realizes the fact that we have passed the stage of colonialism and that we have reached the stage, which has been sneered at at times by certain hon. mem-

bers in this House, of nationhood within the Empire. I believe, Sir, that I could quote very many hon. gentlemen who have used the same expression. One very notable example is the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I have read some of his speeches wherein he made the statement that we have become a nation within the Empire. Mr. Smuts, the Premier of South Africa, has used the same expression. I cannot help but think sometimes when I hear the speeches of some hon. gentlemen that they seem to desire that we should remain in a backward state. At such times I cannot help recalling an expression used by the present Prime Minister of Canada, I think it was about three years ago, which expression struck me very strongly at the time. It was the expression that such speeches are a strange mixture of colonialism and imperialism run mad. That was the thought that ran through my head today when I listened to one or two speeches that were made by hon. gentlemen -on the other side of this question.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition made one observation which struck me as worth mentioning, although I do not pretend to have any particular knowledge of. international affairs. He criticised very severely the idea that at times the Canadian representative at Washington, if he were appointed, should take over the duties of the British ambassador. I do not see that there is anything more strange in that than in what happens continually in international affairs. For example: suppose that a war broke out between the United States and Spain. Then the Spanish ambassador would leave the United States and he would hand over his affairs to, we will say, the British ambassador, or to the German ambassador, or to the Dutch ambassador. It certainly would be no more strange, it seems to me, for such a representative of Canada in Washington, for a very short time-it would only be for a short time on any occasion-to handle the affairs of Britain, to represent the British ambasador, as that ambassador on many occasions, and the representatives of other nations, handle the affairs of nations with which they really have no connection such as we have with the British Empire.
Sir, I believe that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) expressed the opinion of Western Canada when he said that this was a question in which we are interested, and when he further said that this was an idea which he thought would
benefit Canada if caried out in a proper manner.
Sir, the Canadian people took such a proud position in this war as to prove that they are the equals in war of any other people. I do not think that the Canadian people are willing to admit that in peace they are inferior to other people. If we are not to gradually progress along the lines upon which we are advancing, along lines I am bound to confess piloted by the right hon. gentleman who recently resigned from the leadership of this Government, then we would remain in a colonial state which to most Canadians is an unsatisfactory state. We would remain in the position which, even when I was a young boy, was one of humiliation to me. For example, at international conferences when Canadian representatives would take an inferior position as compared with the representatives of Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Bulgaria, or Siam, or perhaps some of the South American or Central republics,
I used to feel humiliated. To-day thanks to the efforts of our representatives at the Peace Conference, Canadian representatives have been given a status which is enjoyed by representatives of other nations of the world, and we no longer occupy the inferior position which we did occupy up to very recently at international conferences or gatherings of any kind.
Sir, I do not wish to take any more of of the time of the House except to say in closing, that I believe very sincerely in the idea of having a Canadian representative at Washington-always with the point in view that he is not to tear us away from the ties which bind us to the British Empire; because I do not think that anybody will accuse any of the hon. gentlemen who are piloting this Bill, or who have supported the measure, of any desire to separate Canada from the British Empire. Always keeping that in view, I believe that a Canadian representative at Washington will have infinitely more interest in Canadian affairs. The right hon. member from King's (Sir Robert Borden) said to-day that Mr. Bryce had stated that from two-thirds to three-quarters of the affairs handled by the British Embassy at Washington were Canadian affairs. Why should Canadians hand over their affairs to any appointee of Great Britain rather than have them handled by a Canadian representative always acting in close co-operation witn the British representative? Mr. Chairman, I have very great pleasure, so far as I am concerned, as a humble representative

of the middle west of Canada, in supporting this proposition to have a Canadian representative handle the affairs of Canada in the United States capital.	[DOT]

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do
not propose to take up much of the time of the committee but as previous speakers have deemed it necessary to express their personal opinions in regard to the subject before us I feel that I should state what my own views are. I need not tell hon. gentlemen that I am very proud of being a British subject and a Canadian, and I am old fashioned enough to be prouder of being a British subject than being a Canadian. Although born on Canadian soil and proud of Canadian institutions I was taught from my youth to be prouder of the British flag and all it stood for than anything else that I could claim as my own. Consequently I do not feel any humiliation whatever when I require assistance as a Britisher in the United States, if I call upon the British consul. I do not think that that is in any way belittling my position.
But before proceeding any further with the subject, let me offer my congratulations to the right hon. member for King's County, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), for the very able and excellent presentation of the case which he' made this afternoon.
I have known the right hon. gentleman for a long time and I know that he will present any subject he touches at all in good shape and as strongly as it can be done before any tribunal that he is addressing. But while congratulating him in that respect I must also congratulate him more upon the tremendous strides he has made in regard to what we can do in Canada and what our status is. Both of us were young men at one time in this House, he of course occupying a higher and more prominent position than I do, but I remember his speeches very well for the last seventeen years. It is not more than half of that period since I heard the right hon. gentleman saying in this House that we could not build ships in Canada-we had not the men, nor the material, nor the brains, nor the capacity to do anything of the kind. If we could attempt such a thing it would take fifty years for us to get into the position of being able to do it, and by that time those of us in the House would be dead and resting in our graves. That was the opinion of my right hon. friend at that time, and he told us that if we wanted to do anything that would attract attention in the great Empire to which we belong the right thing to do was to send i' M r Manion.]
thirty-five or forty millions of money across to the Old Country where we could buy ships, and get the British Government to man them and send them up to the North Sea where they were most needed. Mf right hon. friend is to be congratulated upon the change of heart he has since experienced-such a change of heart that he is now satisfied that not only can we build ships and get the men to man them, not only have we the material but we are so independent of the Mother Country that we can launch out on our own account, have our own army, have our own navy, have our own system of defence, and have our own plenipotentiary at Washington. Perhaps in such a short space of time there never was a greater change in the life history and practice of any hon. gentleman than that which is found in the case of my right hon. friend, and I claim with pride that we both come from the same province.
Now, as to the necessity of this new departure, I do not myself, Sir, see ai'y necessity for it. I submit that every interest of Canada is well looked after at Washington by the British ambassador, and that we avoid a great deal of responsibility and worry as a result. As a dominion at our best we have no power to declare war or peace. If we do declare war upon any country, we cannot back it up, for we have not got the army or the navy requisite for the purpose. I am not belittling our country because we have not the men and the equipment for warlike undertakings-we are not looking for trouble, and we see no necessity for war. But if war conditions should arise, or if we are implicated in a matter which must be settled by war, that war must be declared by the Mother Country, and the British navy and the British army will be behind us. If that condition arose, for instance, with the United States, we would know that it had been brought about through the agency of the British ambassador, that he knew what was developing and was making representations to his Government. But if we are going to cut loose from the wisdom and experience of British diplomacy, and our own inexperienced diplomat gets us into trouble, what assurance have we got that we are immediately goiing to have the British army and navy behind us? Are not those things worth preserving? Is it not worth while to continue the old practice under which we have prospered and are so happy and contented? I feel that there is not the slightest necessity for this departure at

all. Being represented in the United States to-day by the British ambassador, we have behind us all the prestige and power of the British Empire. Are we going to improve our position by severing ourselves from that association and sending a representative of our own to Washington? What will be behind the representative of Canada? We are proud of ourselves, but surely we cannot for one moment say that we can put behind our solitary lone ambassador the strength, force and dignity which we now share as part of the British Empire whose ambassador is our representative.
That is the stand I take, Mr. Chairman. The Canadian people are happy and contented in governing themselves to their heart's content. Why, Sir, we have such freedom of government that to-day we have a Government which we on this side of the House believe is absolutely incapable of governing us at all, but we can revel in a luxury of that kind! Holding these views, old-fashioned if you please, but such views as have stood the test of ages, I would be slow to depart from them and to launch upon any new experiment which in my judgment is absolutely unnecessary.
I yield to no man in my desire for the most absolute liberty for every Canadian consistent with our obligations as citizens of the Empire, but I do not feel that the ties which bind us to the Mother Country chafe us in any way. We are perfectly happy and contented under the machinery created by the British Crown. That being the case, if a vote was to be cast upon this question, I would feel obliged to say that I would vote against it. I may differ slightly with my leader in this matter and with other gentlemen in this House, but this is an occasion when I claim to exercise my own judgment and to express my own views.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been such a wide divergence of opinion on this subject that for once I feel quite at liberty to follow the example of my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat (Mr. McKenzie) and differ somewhat from my leader. I agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and I wish to associate myself with him in offering to my right hon. friend, the member for King's, N.S., the ex-Prime Minister of this country, hearty congratulations-in which I am sure the committee will join-on his ability to give evidence of a complete restoration to health by an hour and a half's speech in this House.
That speech was a valuable historic survey of many debates of previous years, which I have no doubt will be referred to by future generations in connection with the debate of to-day.
I noted particularly a phrase in the speech which, perhaps, I may be permitted to commend to the consideration of my hon. friend from Brantfoird (Mr. Cock-shutt). There were many quotations of the greatest interest. I was very much struck with the prescience and the farsightedness of men like Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Mills and others of the political fathers who begat us, as to the gradual evolution which was to take place in the institutions of this country. The phrase from Sir John A. Macdonald to which I should like to call the attention of my hon. friend from Brantford was one in which that famous statesman referred to the necessity of Canada gaining an access to the markets of the world and so promoting the extension of her prosperity. We gain access to the markets of the world, I need not tell my hon. friend from Brantford, sometimes to buy and sometimes to sell; and I am glad to quote to him an authority that he would be the last to question in support of views which I never lose a reasonable opportunity of commending to the intelligence' of the House of Commons of Canada.
I was very much pleased at another of the infrequent incursions of my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Rowell) into the debate. I see rumours in the papers that my hon. friend contemplates retiring from public life. If he had been present I would have advised him to go slowly in that matter, for I think his retirement from the public life of this country would be a very great loss. We are in times of upheaval, and there may be very great changes in the personnel of the next House of Commons. Though I have had my differences and disagreements with my hon. friend from Durham, I should like to be permitted to say across the floor of this House that I do not think Canada can easily dispense with a man who has his record, his fearless courage in support of his convictions, his ability as a debater, and his other splendid qualities calculated to do the highest service in the public life of this country.
Now, may I be permitted to say that we are in a somewhat curious position in debating this subject inasmuch as the proposal which is viewed with so much suspicion by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) emanates, in

the first instance anyhow, from those who cannot be suspected of any weak adherence to the Imperial tie, whereas some of the strongest resistance to the proposal has come from those who are supposed to be suspected in this matter. I do not wish to press the point further than to say that I trust in our approaches to this question and to all the questions that will engage Canada and her representatives in the future so full of anxiety-and I think also so full of hope-that lies immediately in front of us, we shall not cast aspersions upon any sections of political thought in this connection. I am quite sure we ail want to take the step that is in the best interests of our common country and that we are all proud of the record of our soldiers, proud of the flag which floats over us and floats wherever the sun shines.
Now, up to the present, Mr. Chairman, I have not been convinced that evidence has been afforded that the change proposed is going to make for practical benefit along the line on which I directed a question to my hon. friend from Durham at the end of his speech. I asked him for illustrations of questions which would be settled better in the interests of Canada under this new arrangement that is proposed than they are settled at the present time. He gave [DOT]me one illustration, the question about pulp last year. . Well, I never heard that our Government was lax in its duty in regard to that situation. I thought they were active in the matter and that everything that could be done by governmental interference and helpfulness was done to remedy that pulp situation. I cannot share the view so airily expressed by my hon. friend that if we had had a representative of this nature at Washington, the pulp difficulty would have disappeared with any greater rapidity than it did disappear- if, indeed, it has disappeared up to the present moment. I do not find that the illustration carries me very far in this matter, and I cannot myself think of matters in connection with the relationships of Canada and the United States in which we should be immediately helped by the appointment of a minister plenipotentiary.
It is a common enough practice, and I think a somewhat useless one, to speculate upon the ultimate political destiny of this country. Three things are possible. We might unite with the United States. Personally, I feel on very safe ground when I say that that is the least likely destiny for Canada politically. I feel very much inclined for once, in a way, ro become a pro-
IMr M. Clark.]
phet and to say that will not happen, anyhow. We may possibly in the long course of years become an independent country, a sovereign state. That is quite a possibility, but if it does happen it will be, as my right hon. friend indicated this afternoon, by a process of evolution. For my part, Mr. Chairman, I am content for the moment that Canada should remain pretty much where she is. I think the worst foes of the British Empire are those who imitate the little girl who has planted a flower and is always pulling it up to see how its roots are doing. The British Empire is all right; it is in a very healthy condition-and it showed it in the recent events of the world-if people will only leave it alone. It is doing very well, and I think that for an immediate destiny that is sufficient. That is my view; I would leave this process of evolution largely in the hands of the gods for the moment. We have enough to do in the process of reconstruction; enough to do as statesmen; enough to do as members of Parliament; enough to do as individual citizens of Canada, in devoting our fullest attention patriotically to the building up of our own country, the restoration of our national finances and the repairing of the damage which we inevitably suffered by our participation in the great war.
Now, coming to the question under immediate discussion, I recur to the fact that it is by a process of evolution that these changes are to be brought about. Well, Mr. Chairman, I want to say 10 p.m. that if we do take this step we are certainly taking an important step in the direction of a very considerable evolution, according to my view.
I listened very carefully to my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) endeavouring to reply to my hon. friend from Brantford-I say endeavouring, because I think he failed to reply to the very considered and firm position which my hon. friend from Brantford took. I think the appointment of a plenipotentiary to a foreign court is a mark of a Sovereign state. That was the position of my hon. friend from Brantford, and I agree with him absolutely and fully upon that question. I am not, aware, Sir, that it has been done in the history of the world except by a .sovereign state; therefore, my hon. friend was upon extremely strong ground, historically and constitutionally, when he took that position. If that be so, while it is very well to talk about evolution, am I not right in claiming that if we take this step we are

not following the process of evolution, but we are getting very near to revolution. I throw that out for the consideration of my hon. friend and his Government. I would say that it is a question which they should put very carefully and seriously to themselves and discuss with very great caution and thoroughness before they go any further in this matter. If we appoint a plenipotentiary to Washington, and our good friends from Quebec come here in strength some day and say: "It is all very well to appoint a plenipotentiary to Washington; we feel that we might do a much bigger business with France, and we have blood relationship with France; we admire old France; let us have a plenipotentiary to France."

speechtext: Why should we not?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Logically, why should we not? How can that claim be resisted if Quebec comes to this House and presents it, if any other section of the community or of the House of Commons says: "We are a Sovereign state; we have a plenipotentiary at Washington?" My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) would still be in the humiliating position when he compares Canada as a Sovereign state, with other countries, that his boys would be pointing out to him that while other countries had their plenipotentiaries at Berlin, at Washington and at Paris, we, little Canada, only have a plenipotentiary at Washington, nowhere else; we are still a little country.
May I point out in this connection that this status is a costly affair or it may become a very costly commodity? I have not heard any one except the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), call attention to that point which, perhaps, is the most crucial of all at this particular moment of our history. The entourage of an embassy is one of the finest ways for a nation to spend money that I know of, and if you get ten of them, my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) will need to preach economy more strongly than he has ever done in the history of this country. I should like to impress these thoughts very strongly upon the Administration before they go any further with this business, and I should like to impress them upon my hon. friends opposite who pay income tax. Is that burden sitting lightly upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen opposite? I know the farmers are paying income tax, and while in the West they do not begrudge it and prefer direct taxation to indirect,
nevertheless they feel the burden of it, and they do not want to incur any of it which is not necessary, especially at this period.
If I talked all night, I do not think I could say any more to make my point of view clearer. The Government should not hurry in this business; they have not the money. I should be glad to be contradicted in that by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry "Drayton). As the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) says, we are doing very well; we are going on very well as a nation. Let evolution have its own course in this matter. Evolution is a very slow thing; it goes on step by step. Do not let us do this by way of a kick or a jump. Let evolution go slowly; do not be in a hurry about this business. We have enough to do, in the face of the coming Budget, to cover the expenses of the nation that are absolutely necessary at the present time, without taking a step which may lead to eight or ten other steps and hurry us into expenditures which would be very serious for the fortunes of this country, or which many of us might regret. There is no hurry. Let that be the last word I drop on the ears of the Administration. There is no hurry in this matter.

speechtext:
Perhaps I might be excused for rising to speak on this question when I say that I have only a word or two to add to what has already been said. My object in rising is to endeavour to elucidate a certain point, or, at least, to request the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), who will no doubt speak at the end of the debate, to make clear a question which is far from being clear to my mind at the present time. The item now under discussion reads:
Canadian representation in the United States.
It will seem obvious to all who have listened to this debate that there is a considerable divergence of opinion as to the character of the personage who will be sent to Washington to represent Canada. I have heard as many as six designations given of this gentleman. Perhaps there are more, but the notes I have taken give me these. Some have called him a trade agent; others, trade commissioner, others, consular agent, others, consul; others have gone to the length of calling him ambassador and finally some have called him plenipotentiary. It is evident that some of these words have more or less the same meaning; but on the other hand, there is a fundamental difference between a trade

agent and an ambassador or a plenipotentiary, and if the discussion has been so wide on the subject now before the committee, that is because, to a eertain extent, the Government did not see fit at the outset to disclose, exactly and in concrete form, the status and exact functions of the gentleman to be appointed.
I have listened with great pleasure to the addresses made before the committee this afternoon by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell). These hon. members, and in particular the hon. member for Durham, have given a clear definition of the functions which will be fulfilled by the person to be appointed at Washington. Unfortunately, these hon. gentlemen are no longer members of the Government, and therefore, their declarations cannot be taken as an official declaration of the Government. I would humbly request the Prime Minister, when he rises to close the debate, to give a clear definition of the functions of the representative of Canada who will be sent to Washington.
Speaking for myself alone, I am in sympathy with the project of sending a representative to Washington. We cannot ignore the fact that our destinies are not independent of those of the United States. If they be independent politically, they are not independent commercially. No one can deny that our destinies are tied up with the destinies of the United States commercially. This assertion is strongly borne out by the fact that we are doing at the present time more trade with the United States than with any other country in the world, and it would be correct to say that our trade with the United States is nearly equal to our trade with all the other nations of the world. The figures are not absolutely exact, but they are sufficiently accurate to render clear my idea. Consequently, taking into consideration the fact, which no one can deny, that we have this powerful neighbour on which we are unfortunately to a certain extent commercially dependent, not a f^ct which we are willing to assume, but a condition which is being imposed on us, we have to cope with this situation , and in order to cope with this situation, which is unique in the case of Canada as regards all other countries, we should be justified in adopting a unique procedure to meet this unique exigency. Perhaps hon. members are too apt to forget that we are actually losing $100,000,000 on exchange with the United States alone each year. We are buying from the United States at the

present time about one billion dollars' worth of goods each year. Now if you take into consideration the fact that in the past year the exchange between Canada and the United States has varied frorr eight and a fraction, the lowest, to nineteer and one quarter per cent, the highest, saj an average of thirteen or fourteen pet cent on our money, it means that on that one billion dollars' worth of goods that we have bought in twelve months we have made a present of $130,000,000 to the United States. How is it that we are making this present? The answer is very simple. We have to give the United States $113 for every $100 worth of goods that we buy from them. Therefore, unless we should admit that our dollar is not worth 100 cents, we are giving a present of $13 to the United States on every $100 worth of goods that we buy from them. These dollars that we pay to the United States will have to be redeemed. Our currency will have to be placed on a par, if it is not on a par now; and the day that oUr dollar is worth 100 cents in the United States, it will appear that we have given this present to the United States. I am not saying this in the way of criticism. It has many times been said that the Government should see that the exchange should be rectified or equalized, and of course, if that object could be secured it would be a very great thing for Canada, but it is a fact that all countries that took part in the war are placed in a similar position, and Canada along with the others has suffered a depreciation in her currency. Therefore, since the conditions as between this country and the United States are exceptional, since we cannot change those conditions, and since we have to trade with the United States, and give them this enormous present, it is worth while making some sacrifice to have a representative in Washington who will look after Canadian interests and see to it that we get the best possible conditions obtainable with respect to our goods, and perhaps also with respect to our money. I am not saying that if we had a representative at Washington he could equalize the exchange between the two countries, or even reduce the adverse exchange against us, but there is one thing certain, and that is that we have everything to gain from having a direct relationship with the United States through a representative of this kind, and we have a lot to lose if we do not have such a representative.

The right hon. the Prime Minister said in the course of his remarks, in a rather jocular way, that he was looking for a good man to send to Washington. I would not presume to offer him advice, hut with the consent of the hon. member for Durham, I might say that I had the advantage of seeing the work that he did at the Labour Conference at Washington in the month of November 1919. I was in Washington myself during the conference, I had the privilege of assisting at its sittings, and I must do my hon. friend from Durham the justice of saying that he represented Canada in a most creditable manner and with distinction to himself and our country. Therefore, if the Prime Minister is looking for a representative-of course, I do not know whether the hon. member for Durham would accept-but if, for the sake of his country, he would accept, I would recommend him to the Prime Minister.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I will sum up in a sentence, my conclusion: in view of the clear definition that the Prime Minister has given of our status, and of the work to be accomplished by this representative, and of the conditions under which he will act, I think the House should be satisfied to vote for this Estimate.
