I should like,
Mr. Chairman, to say just one word in reply to some observations that have fallen from my hon. friend from Red Deer, because it is just possible that he may be under a misapprehension as to what this proposal really amounts to. The minister who is to be sent to Washington will be appointed by a sovereign power. That sovereign power is the King, who represents the whole Empire. Perhaps I could make my meaning in that regard a little plainer if I should point out this analogy to my hon. friend from Red Deer: We made a treaty between Canada and the United States with respect to the control of boundary waters and the arrangements in connection with them. Commissioners representing Canada were appointed under the provisions of that treaty. They represent Canada as distinctly as if they were appointed by Order in Council, but they are appointed by a sovereign power, the King, who appoints them upon the nomination of the King's Privy Council for Canada. The members of the International Joint Commission do not in one sense exercise diplomatic functions, but they exercise certain functions which are very closely allied thereto. I for one cannot see,
and I do not think my hon. friend the member for Red Deer will be able to see, any distinction between the principle upon which the British Empire acts in the one case and in the other. The King, being the King of Canada as well as of the United Kingdom, will see fit to appoint a minister who will be especially charged to concern himself with and to safeguard the interests of Canada in respect of her relations with the United States. That minister will be responsible to the King's Privy Council for Canada and to the Canadian Parliament. Therefore, I cannot agree that the principle of sovereignty is affected more in this case than in the appointment of the Canadian members of the International Joint Commission.
I should like to emphasize what has been said by the hon. member for Marquette, that every advanced step in extending our rights of self-government has led to more or less apprehension. I ventured some years ago to endeavour to trace those steps in a speech which I delivered on the subject, and I pointed out what is absolutely true, that in every case the enlargement of the sphere of selfgovernment in this and the other Dominions has led to closer ties than those which existed before. I am quite sure that the confidence of the Government of the United Kingdom is sanctioning and supporting this arrangement, a confidence reposed in the good sense and canacity of the people of Canada to conduct their own affairs, will strengthen, instead of weakening, the ties that bind us to the Mother Country, and the rest of the Empire; and I venture the hope that in the outcome my hon. friend the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), whom I thank very heartily for his kind reference to myself, will reach the conclusion that this further step in advance is one that will be attended with advantage to the unity of the Empire.

speechtext:
I shall not attempt to prolong the debate at any length. We have listened to-day to one of the most interesting discussions that have ever taken place in this House. I am the more pleased at what I have heard this afternoon and evening because this is probably the first time that members in this House have spoken their mind freely on the question of the future of this Dominion. Mr. Chairman, before I discuss the point which was so ably taken a moment ago by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), let me say a word about the item under

discussion. I shall vote in favour of that item. Some years ago I was probably one of the first to state that the time had come for Canada to appoint, not an ambassador or a semi-ambassador, but a representative in Washington, the capital of the great neighbouring Republic. Our interests are so intermingled, our trade with that country is so large, and, besides, there are so many connections in various ways, that nature and sentiment alike compel both countries to seek the closest possible relations. When the question came up a few years ago I said that in my recol-. lection the late leader of the Liberal party (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), to my certain knowledge, had in mind the appointment of a high commissioner in Washington. I do not say that the question was ever broached in Council, but it is a matter of common knowledge that he favoured the appointment of a very distinguished Canadian to that high position. He thought that Canada should be well represented in London, in Paris, and in Washington. Events so transpired that he could not realize his plan, but I say again, with a sense of responsibility, that he had on various occasions expressed the desire that some day Canada should be represented by a high commissioner in Washington.
Mr. Chairman, I do believe that a high commissoner would be more useful than an ambassador at Washington, unless, as stated a moment ago by my hon. friend from Red Deer, we choose to cut the painter at once and proclaim Canada an independent nation; because you cannot have an ambassador in any foreign country unless you exercise that essential power of sovereignty which Canada does not possess. This is the A. B. C. of international law, and it is merely deluding ourselves, it seems to me, to pretend that Canada can under present conditions appoint an ambassador or a minister plenipotentiary to a foreign country. I think that neither the right hon. gentleman from King's (Sir Robert Borden), nor the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), who is Minister for External Affairs, will for one moment contend that Canada can of her own initiative, under the powers that belong to her and which are contained in the Canadian constitution, appoint an ambassador to any foreign country, or a minister plenipotentiary. Now, let us not delude ourselves; let us face realities and not shams. Can we or can we not appoint that ambassador? Can we or can we not appoint that minister plenipotenrMr. Lemieux.]
tiary? Can we or can we not negotiate and sign a treaty without the rightful interference of the Foreign Office in London, or of the British ambassador or Minister-it depends on the status of the country-with which	we are
engaged in negotiating such a treaty? In spite of the boast of my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), that Canada had reached the status of nationhood and could, as soon as she pleased, appoint an ambassador and consuls, the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce ((Sir George Foster) laid upon the table of the House a Treaty with France, whereon we saw appended to it the signature of the British ambassador in Paris. I read the correspondence of the right hon. gentleman and of the Minister of Justice with the British authorities regarding the signature to be appended to that treaty.
Why all this play at nationhood, when, as a matter of fact, we have none of the powers that belong to a nation unless we solemnly declare that we are a nation and live up to that declaration. This is putting the facts plainly and squarely before the House.	,
But to come back to the question under consideration, I will support by my vote this evening the appointment of a Canadian representative in Washington. Mr. Chairman, we cannot legislate against geopraphy. We have too much business in the United States and our trade operations are too immense to be ignored. I believe that we can foster a broader spirit of brotherhood and a closer friendship between the two countries if we are represented there by a man who, as was said this afternoon by my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Rowell), could explain to the American authorities our point of view, our sentiments, and even our exigencies in relation to certain questions affecting both countries. My hon. friend from Red Deer spoke of the possibilities of the future. Shall it be the statu quo? Shall it be union with the American Republic? Or shall it be the independence of Canada?
Mr. Chairman, I am speaking for myself. I do not believe that any man in this House dreams of a permanent statu quo; there is a stage of evolution for a nation as for an individual. The fruit must ripen and when the fruit has ripened it falls from the parent tree. I will do nothing to revolutionize, but I am quite willing to evolutionize-to await the destiny of Canada, leaving it in the hands of Divine

Providence that shapes the destinies of men and nations alike. But let me say this to the Government: when the time comes for Canada to take the decisive step which shall lead her to nationhood, I for one shall stand for Canada as a kingdom. The desire was expressed by Sir John A. Macdonald, the greatest of the Fathers of Confederation, that Canada should be a kingdom and that a member of the Royal Family in England should be the King of Canada. I stand by the views of Sir John A. Macdonald on that question. But, Sir,
I warn my fellowmen that if Canada is to avoid the other alternative, that of annexation with the United States, we must, as Canadians, watch carefully the economic situation. To-day the Americans are peacefully invading our prairies. I do not object to them-they are excellent farmers in the West; indeed I believe they are the best farmers in the West together with our own Canadian native-born. They also are invading our cities in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec, with their capital, which is flowing in all directions. Therefore, from the standpoint, American capital controls, to a large degree the financial future of this country. And besides-and now I sneak as a Canadian of French descent-English speaking Canada-that is to say eight provinces out of nine, have practically the same laws as they have across the border -eight provinces out of nine speak the same language, uniform system of schools, and-if I read aright in the press and if I judge by theatres, cinema pictures and other productions much the same ideals, the same frame of mind, the same accent and -even Mr. Chairman, the same twang. English speaking Canada in that sense, is becoming Americanized in spite of all.
While we are racially divided-and there are some fools in this country always ready, to kindle the fires of race hatred

if my English-speaking fellowmen are anxious to keep this country British, my advice to them is: treat the French-Cana-dian minority gently and generously. Sir John A. Macdonald followed that course and his friends at the time of Confederation did likewise. Mr. Pope, the father of Senator Pope, also understood it. He was one of the best men that ever sat in this House, although he was not much given to public speaking, and his effort in the form of a certain phrase is well known. After an eloquent speech in which the late Edward Blake charged Mr. Pope with something I do not remember what, in the administration of the Railway Department, Mr. Pope simply rose from his seat and, in his quaint way, said, "Mr. Speaker, there ain't nothin' to it." That was his style of eloquence. Mr. Pope- the Minister of Trade and Commerce knew him well; he was probably in the same Government with him-was a man of judgment, he was one of those David Harums of the Eastern Townships who had lots of common sense, native ability, and industry. Mr. Pope never failed to say to his English-speaking friends, "You wish to keep this country British? Very well, plant French-Canadian colonies here and there across the continent and treat them generously." That is what he himself did in his own county of Compton. All along the border of Vermont he favoured the establishment of French-Canadian parishes and parishes grew, because population grows where you have French-Canadians and all over there you have to-day a strong and healthy Canadian sentiment. Now this advice is given free of charge to my hon. friends. I tell them-it is a wholesome truth I am preahing-if Canada is to remain British, be tolerant with the French-Canadians, treat them generously, not only in their so-called reserve of Quebec, but all over Canada, for they are your equals. Do not bully them. It is the fashion of some of my Englishspeaking friends, because they are in the majority, because they are the conquering race to lord it over the minority. My English-speaking friends are not all of the same frame of mind, I know, but there are too many imbued with that idea of domination. If you want to make this Dominion a country worthy to live in, get the two races united on a basis of equality, grant them their rights and their privileges and you will have a Dominion to be proud of.

speechtext:
There is the other
alternative, the Imperial Federation scheme, which would bring about, I suppose, a centralized government. Splendid idea! Full of grandeur! But very difficult of realization. Then under that plan, you would have a voice in the affairs of the Empire, but your voice would only be proportionate to your strength in the representation of that federated parliament of the Empire; and it would mean in the long run that your defence- the army and the navy of the Empire

would be controlled by a central parliament in London where you would have but a few votes or a few representatives

to give effect to your views. Then what would happen? A conflict would arise, because Britishers the world over are first of all liberty-lovers, and out of such conflict might come the breakup of the whole Imperial fabric. My hon. friends know their history, they know how the independence of the United States was brought about: it was a case of some such conflict between the Mother Country and the Thirteen Colonies. The same thing would happen in the event of a conflict of interests in that central parliament. As I said a moment ago, the evolution will come slowly and every year Canada will get a broader vision. If you are anxious to maintain that happy state of things, let well enough alone, and above all have a keen respect for the autonomy of the Dominions. Because it is one of the merits of the British system of government that the autonomy of the component parts is absolute and complete, and Britishers themselves grow very restless and sensitive when that autonomy is in question. Make haste slowly, but above all, respect the traditions of all your fellow citizens, be moderate in your views, do not bully the minority, have regard to the failings of the minorities-their prejudices, and thus you will have peace in the Dominion.
The evolution is coming step by step. You cannot arrest it; it is a law of nature. The time comes for a nation, as for an individual, to shape its own destiny. When a young man has lived with his parents until the age of twenty-one, he has to cut the home moorings and start a home for himself. After all, would it not be the pride and the glory of the Mother Country to see the Dominions which sprang form her loins gradually increasing their activities and enlarging their potentialities and having rooted in their respective soils the standards and the ideals of life that have made the Mother Country herself the great nation she is, steer their own course.

Mr. Chairman, this question is undoubtedly one of the largest and most involved that has been discussed in the Canadian Parliament since I first became a member of it, and at the outset I should like to congratulate the committee for discussing it in such a dispassionate way. We have witnessed to-day an admirable spectacle, that of hon. members discussing a problem not only of Canadian, but of international importance, in a spirit of brotherhood and with a calmness which is highly to be commended.
For a number of years Canada has had a High Commissioner in Paris, but to-day Canada is represented in no foreign country other than France. It may strike one as surprising that Canada, being in the immediate neighbourhood of the greatest republic in the world and having with that republic almost boundless trade relations, never before last year thought of being represented in Washington. At the last session a departure in our political life was announced in the House-that Canada should appoint to Washington a minister plenipotentiary whose duty it would be to attend exclusively to matters arising between Canada and the United States. Our representative or our ambassador or our plenipotentiary should, if I understand rightly the declarations that have been made from official quarters, confine himself to Canadian business. What would be the procedure in the matter of the appointment of this plenipotentiary? I have listened with the closest attention to the speeches delivered on this subject from both sides of the House. I have listened carefully to the declaration made by the last speaker (Mr. Keefer), in his very eloquent address, that this appointment would be made not by Canada but by His Majesty

the King. He even pointed out that His Majesty the King of England could appoint a representative of Canada to Washington without even consulting us.

speechtext: I did not state that; you misunderstand my position. The King can only act in Canada, of course, on the advice of his responsible Canadian minister, just as he can only act in the United Kingdom on the advice of his responsible British ministers. Why? The King can do no wrong. It is the ministers only who can do wrong, by their wrong advice as his advisers.

speechtext:
That the King can do no wrong is an obsolete proposition. It is admitted now by men who are conversant with parliamentary life and institutions, that the King can commit some wrongs. I am sorry if I have misunderstood my hon. friend. I certainly construed his words as conveying the idea that the King, even without the recommendation of the Canadian authorities, could appoint a representative at Washington. Be this as my hon. friend says, I stand corrected in this regard, but how is this appointment going to made? We have listened to different speeches, the purport of which was that the Dominions of the British Empire were on an equal footing with the Mother Country. It has been repeatedly said in this House by hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches, that the nations of the British Empire are now equal in status. I beg to differ from this view. There are in the British Empire certain nations that are on an equal footing, and they are the four Dominions, and above and beyond those four nations there is one supreme and sovereign nation, and that is the United Kingdom. Who will contend for one moment that you can appoint a plenipotentiary to Washington by recommending to His Majesty the King that a man be appointed, without that recommendation passing through the channel of the Foreign Office or the British Government? Nobody will contend that. If my right hon. friend who leads the Government (Mr. Meighen) will say to the committee to-day: "We will recommend to His Majesty the King the appointment of a certain gentleman to fill the important post of plenipotentiary at Washington and this recommendation will go direct to His Majesty without remaining for a day or a week or a month in the office of the Secretary for Foreign Affairs or the Secretary for the Colonies in England," then we will accept his statement, and we will say that

Canada has really progressed in her political status. But my right hon. friend will never say that, because it will not be the case. His recommendation, however worthy it may be, will have to pass through the hands of the British Government. I do r[ot say that I object to that; but I strongly and firmly object to the contention that the Dominions and the United Kingdom are politically on an equal footing, because they are not, and it is ridiculous to contend that they are, as my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) pointed out this afternoon.
I am not against appointing a representative at Washington; I favour the proposition most heartily. Why should Canada not be represented at Washington? Canada should be represented at Washington as Canada is represented in France. Such representation carries with it a number of advantages which were presented in a most creditable and instructive manner this afternoon by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell). It carries with it the advantage of being on the spot, the advantage of being in contact with the British Ambassador in Washington every day, the advantage of being in contact with the political personages of the great Capital of the country to the south of us. There are many other advantages which I will not take up the time of the committee to relate; but coupled with those advantages, especially if we appoint a minister plenipotentiary, are many dangers. What dangers? The danger that, even if this representation be confined to purely Canadian affairs, conflicts are bound to arise, perhaps secretly between British interests and Canadian interests. Let us go a few years back in the history of Canada. Who amongst us does not know the fact and incident that, on a certain occasion, Sir John Macdonald, who had been sitting in Washington, returned to Canada and his home disgusted, as he expressed it, at the proceedings there because the Canadian interests had been sacrificed by the British authorities in presence of the Americans? Let us come a little later to the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when the Alaskan boundary question was under discussion. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said a moment ago-and he was supported in that contention, I think, by the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden).- that every step towards antonomy on the part of Canada, though it first had created alarm, had developed into closer and better arrangements and understandings between

the Mother Country and ourselves. These steps that were taken at the time that Sir John Macdonald sat in Washington, these steps that were taken later at the time of the settlement of the Alaskan boundary question, were at a time when Canada was passing gradually from the stage of colonialism of the stage of autonomy. What was the result? I do not want to bring to the attention of the committee the painful spectacle which was offered in Canada at the time of the Alaskan boundary question, when the representative of Canada, sitting in Washington with the British representative and the American representative, was voted down by the two, the American and the British, when he came back to Canada and held, as I think it was called then, a demonstration of protest in the city of Toronto. I do not say that that will be repeated; but when you say that every step towards greater autonomy for Canada makes only for better understandings between the Mother Country and ourselves I say that this is bound to arise and certainly it will arise if my right hon. friend who leads the Government (Mr. Meighen) carries out his idea that this appointment will be of such a nature that the Canadian plenipotentiary will assume the duties of the British ambassador in the case of the British ambassador being absent. I agree with the proposition of appointing a representative at Washington; I may go so far as to agree that a discussion of purely Canadian affairs be confined as between him and the American authorities; but I want to register my opposition against the Canadian plenipotentiary acting at any time, even for one hour, as the representative of the whole British Empire. I object to that because I see in it many dangers.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who always speaks eloquently and whom I was delighted to listen to this afternoon, was saying that it was customary between nations that the ambassador of one nation should take over the interests of another nation. That we know very well. During my visit in the city of Berlin some years ago the interests of the British Empire were entrusted to the American Embassy up to the time the United States entered the war, but does my hon. friend think for a moment that the American ambassador in Berlin would subordinate the interests of his (country to the interests of the British Empire? Not for one moment. Then, in this concrete case, the British 154
interests were subordinate to the American interests, and had the British interests come into conflict with the American interests, what would have been the immediate step of the American ambassador? He would have subordinated the British interests to the American interests.
Let us suppose a case. Let us suppose that my right hon. friend's ambassador in Washington assume the duties of the British ambassador. Let us go one step further, and suppose a case of purely Canadian interests coming into conflict with British interests. .Think for a moment of the disastrous situation that would result if our ambassador should subordinate the British interests to the Canadian interests! If these two cases are parallel, if they are to be assimilated, as my hon. friend said this afternoon, then it would be the duty of our plenipotentiary to subordinate the interests of Great Britain to the interests of Canada. What a situation! No, let us go slowly. My hon. friend from Red Deer closed his remarks with that admonition: Do not hurry, go slowly. He is quite right, but he need not have any apprehensions. The appointment will not be made very soon, and there is a good reason for that, Mr. Chairman. My Fight hon. friend the Prime Minister is in the position of a certain man who had two sisters and did not want to make a choice between them. The poet of Montmartre has said-I know if I quoted him in French my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce would understand me, but perhaps I had better translate-"Between the two sisters my trouble is great. It is not to know to which of the two my heart should address its vows. Both of the sisters are worthy that I should love them, and my trouble comes when I consider which of the two I Shall not like." That is the position of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. He has two pretenders to the position, both very worthy, eminent statesmen. They have this afternoon delivered themselves in such a creditable manner that I realize fully-

speechtext: I accept the statement made by the right hon. gentleman. I am extremely sorry if I hurt the feelings of such an eminent gentleman as the exPrime Minister. Did I say that he was an applicant? I do not remember having used the word, but if I did, it was not by in-, tention. I repeat, he is a worthy Canadian, and he. is a candidate even if he does not wish to be a candidate. In 1917, I was elected without my consent ever being given to being a candidate. That may be the case this time with my right hon. friend. He does not pretend to be the representative of Canada at Washington, but in spite of himself he may have to accept the position, for the sake of Canada, and not to displease his own political friends. Be that as it may, the position of the right hon. the Prime Minister is difficult; we all realize that, and he will postpone the appointment for a very, very long time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I think it is only just to the hon. member for Durham to say that the hon. member for Beauce is entirely wrong as to him also.
[Hr. Fielding.]

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Then nobody will be appointed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am sure I am quite right in saying that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is in a very difficult position when he has such good material to select from. What I want to point out is that outside of these two hon. gentlemen my right hon. friend has many others from whom he could make a good selection. but my hon. friend from Red Deer need have no apprehension; the appointment will not be made very soon.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: If nobody will take the job, it will never be filled.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I confess that I cannot absolutely agree with my hon. friend from Red Deer. I think that Canada should be represented at Washington. During the war Canada had a worthy representative in Paris in the person of the Hon. Mr. Roy. I understand that in its communications with the French Government the Caadian Government used the services of the Hon. Mr. Roy, very properly, not in a purely political sense, but for looking after many matters in connection with the successful carrying on of the war. Let us have a representative at Washington, but do not clothe the gentleman with these wonderful powers that have been enumerated to-day, and which the hon. member for Durham in particular outlined. Let him be a representative of Canada, just as Mr. Roy was the representative of Canada in Paris, and then I think the people will be satisfied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am sorry to delay the committee, but I would be doing a little injustice if I did not explain one or two matters. When I was on my feet and under cross examination at eight o'clock by hon. gentlemen opposite, I made a statement with regard to the tri-partite nature of the negotiations leading up to the arrangement, and I read at the close a statement of the precise position the minister plenipotentiary would be in. I refer my hon. friend from Joliette to that. He will find it in ' Hansard, and it clearly and fully answers the question which he put to me in that regard. In my remarks I used the word "correspondence," and from that it might be deduced that there had been what is ordinarily known as correspondence with the United States. I understand from a closer reading of the memorandum, which I had in mind in making the statement, that there is nothing in the way of formal cor-

respondence. There was, however, informal communication with the United States Government as regards the matter, in order that their mind might be known as to the reception of the minister plenipotentiary when appointed. The correspondence such as there is refers to that, and as it does, the principle is involved of disclosing the nature of these communications, which we have no right to do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: These informal communications which the Prime Minister speaks of were doubtless had with the previous administration. Has he any assurance that the administration which has succeeded will accept the statement that he now puts before the House as representing the situation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
There has been no
communication at all, so far as I know, with regard to the subject occurred when but there would be no difference whatever regarding a matter of that sort. The Secretary of State in the United States Department would not, on any account, as I understand foreign policy, change his attitude in that regard without at least advising us.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
This is the third or
fourth time I have voted for this matter; I think it is the third time. Now, I do not wish to ask my hon. friend whether he is going to make the appointment within two weeks or a month. I would ask him, however, in all sincerity, whether it is the intention of the Government to appoint this representative within this fiscal year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It is not only the intention, but the sincere hope. The reason why this has not been done so far is the reason that has been given-the only reason. To return to the subject with which I was dealing before, the correspondence is fragmentary, in that much of the conversations, as they are described, that took place with regard to the subject occurred when the Prime Minister of the day was overseas and in personal conference. What took place with the United States was much of the same character. There were some telegrams, and I am not sure whether there were letters or not. On careful examination of the telegrams by the legal adviser of the Department of External Affairs, to see whether there were some which we could be justified in bringing down, he decided that there were not. He discusses for a time whether there were two telegrams that might be brought down, but
154i
portions of them were confidential, and he closes his memorandum thus:
To publish a part of the first two telegrams without the rest would be incongruous ; the confidential matter is insepa * rable; the result would be fragmentary and rather meaningless. Accordingly it is submitted that all should be withheld. The public announcement contains the arrangement as reached in the negotiations ;

I would draw attention to the next sentence, because it is expressive of what is a practice applicable not only to this case, but also, apparently, applicable universally to matters of this kind:
-even President Wilson's famous point about "open covenants" did not, according to his own interpretation, require the details of the negotiations of the "covenants" to be published.
So that no country, and not even the late President of the United States, who has pressed the matter of open covenants probably further than it has ever been carried before, has ventured to say that the negotiations leading up to the final result should be published.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
What statement is
the Prime Minister quoting?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am reading from a
memorandum prepared by the legal adviser of the Department of External Affairs, after carefully investigating whether there was anything which the Government had a right to bring down in the way of correspondence leading to the arrangement. There could be nothing in the world of advantage to the committee in the negotiations; the important question is: what was the final result? The proposal and counterproposal could not be interesting in this case, and could not be of any value to us in deciding whether or not the arrangement, as finally agreed upon, was a proper one. In these matters we must be governed by the practice of governments and by the best advice of those who have given careful and, indeed, lifelong study to the subject.
I have nothing to add to the general debate. It has been taken care of on both sides of the House by those who have given probably more time to the general question than I have. I only want to say that while I do not follow the arguments of hon. gentlemen who oppose the vote, I have not heard any speech on the part of any one who opposes it that does not disclose a sentiment with which I am in full harmony and accord. Indeed, if I may say so, I feel myself in point of sentiment in accord with

those who oppose the vote, but, in point of reason, in sympathy with those who support it. If I thought that the step which this vote contemplates was a step towards withdrawal from the Empire, or a loosening of the bonds that bind us to the Empire, I could bo relied upon to be among the first of those who would oppose it and would consistently do so at all costs. I do not so regard it. Indeed, the reasoning of the member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie), seems to me to he very impressive indeed. This step is one that should make even better the relations between the countries, because it is a step in the direction of fuller autonomy; it is a step in the evolution of our status as a nation; and each step in the past has been accompanied by progress in strength of the real bond that binds the Empire together.
I cannot follow the reasoning which leads to the conclusion that we must maintain colonial status or else march towards the disintegration of the Imperial structure. That does not appeal to me in any degree. Indeed, the Imperial structure has multiplied in strnegth as the different Dominions of the Empire have elevated themselves step by step beyond the colonial status. Nor do I think that this will be the end of the evolution of the Dominion into nationhood. I cannot conceive that even the relationship that this establishes would be adequately expressive of what the position of this Dominion should be in relation to the rest of the Empire when, say, we have a population here equal to the population of the United Kingdom. All this will take care of itself with the passage of time. What we are doing now is to take a step in relation to permanent representation at Washington, parallel to that which we took in relation to the treaty making power, having representatives of this country really negotiate treaties and advise His Majesty in relation thereto; and paralel to the step we have taken in respect of the International Joint Commission, where Canada virtually negotiates with the United States but where the representatives are representatives of the sovereign power, its head being the King, named on the advice of his ministers for this country. We are simply taking another step akin to those already taken, and this time in regard to our permanent representation at Washington, the capital of the great republic to the south. Nor does it follow, because we take this step in relation to the United States, that it would be even natural for us to take it in relation to other

countries. It may be so, in the course of the long years, we know not when; but our position with regard to the United States differs most substantially from our position in relation to any other country in the world. We are alongside of them; we necessarily have more intimate relations with them, and we have a far vaster intercourse with them of every kind, commercial, diplomatic and all the rest, than we do with any other country. There is no reason at all from which you can argue that because we take this tep in relation to that country we must go on and incur the expense of having diplomatic representatives in the various capitals of Europe or other countries of the world. It has been urged very strongly on the part of one hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) that what we should be doing is to create consular agencies, trade agencies, in the United States instead. Well, something can be said against that particularly from the standpoint of-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I did not say "instead."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

Perhaps that is not
necessary to the argument I am trying to make.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

I said "in conjunction
with" in order to make it useful.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I have very much
sympathy with that idea myself.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: What idea?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: With the idea of having, when it can be thoroughly worked out, consular representation there; that is to say for the purposes that we have heard about to-night. But something can be argued against that from a standpoint that cannot be taken against this proposition, in that it may be said that if we have representatives there whose duty it is to do what the United States representatives do here in relation to trade, charging fees for so doing and thereby becoming to an extent an impediment, when we do that we should do it for other countries; otherwise it can be said it would be discrimination against Europe. As regards this proposition, that cannot be argued at all. There Is nothing that leads us into any further step at all because we take this step in relation to the United States. We do it there because of our close kinship, commercially, diplomatically and every other way with that great country, differing wholly in our relationship with other countries in the world.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
How does
my right hon. friend reconcile that argument with the argument we have heard previously to the effect that we are doing it because of our national status? Does not national status relate to every country in the world-?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not say we are
doing it because of our national status.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
But others
have said so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I do not know that they have but at any rate it is a matter of expression. We are doing it because we need it, because it is going to be of service to us.	__

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: For trade?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: We need it for several reasons; it is not trade alone.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The Minister
of Finance said the other day that we had plenty of trade with the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I do not think he said that we had plenty of trade with the United States, but do not divert me from my subject. I am ready to discuss trade with the hon. gentleman, I have done so before. We are doing this because we believe we need it. We believe we need this representative in Washington for purposes that are Canadian ; and a better example could scarcely have been offered the hon. member for Red Deer than that proposed to him by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell). If he had to do with the matter referred to as I had to do with it, he would have seen the value of having a permanent representative there. The difficulty in that regard, and it applies to similar difficulties in the future, might well have been avoided had we had a representative at Washington at that time fully conversant with the situation in Canada and with the real reasons that influenced the Government of Canada in relation to that matter. But I do not want to wander from the subject. We take this step not because we are a nation and merely to express our nationhood. We take it for the service it is going to be to us. We take it because it will be a help to us, but it does illustrate the growing nationhood of the country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It does illustrate the
development of this country as an integral portion of the Empire; it 'illustrates the evolution of this Empire as an Empire.
But it is not merely for the purpose of so illustrating it that we take the step. If it has no purpose and utility it should not have been done. That is all I desire to say.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Have we any constitutional right to make an appointment to the United States that is not of equal force with regard to any nation in Europe? Have we any inherent right as a people, or any power, to make that appointment, that we do not possess in the case of other nations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Not at all. The United States as a foreign country is in just the same position as regards Canada as any other country; and if the need arises to do likewise with any other country-if the need arises equally great and equally pressing-why then, of course, we will have the same right to do it in the same way.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not wish at this late hour to detain the committee at any length, but there are two or three views to which I would like to give expression, particularly as reference has been made by several speakers to my own remarks in the matter. In the first place I may be permitted for a moment to emphasize again the rather remarkable situation in which we find ourselves when-in a matter of vast importance, a matter of exceptional importance involving as some say a material change in the status of the country-we are without a scrap of information as to the correspondence that has passed. I do not know any previous transaction that has ever been presented to this House, at all approaching it in importance, without the history of the negotiations being submitted to us. If the right hon. gentleman cannot give us that correspondence, all I can say is that it is a great misfortune, and it is a very strange way to inaugurate a great change in our relations both Imperial and domestic. It is a misfortune that my right hon. friend has to say, "It is a great change, but we cannot tell you how it came about."
There is another curious fact in connection with this matter. The information given us to-day in the very interesting presentation contributed by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), showed that for many years there has been talk of this. There has been for a long period talk of negotiating our own treaties and incidentally, in many cases, reference has been made and the proposal has been advanced that we should have a Canadian

representative at Washington, but in every case the proposal has been turned down. For thirty years or more this has been talked about, but the judgment of the governments of both sides, and of all parties, and of all the statesmen of the country, after full consideration, has been to turn down the proposition. During those thirty years or more we have at all times been struggling-perhaps I should not say that-but we have been making an effort to bring about closer trade relations with the United States. There have been during this period perhaps some reasons stronger than exist to-day for having somebody to represent Canada at Washington. During all these thirty years the leading purpose of every government has been to try to bring about closer trade relations with the United States, but during all that time every government has turned this proposition down. Now we are taking it up at a time when, to put it mildly, we have less desire to trade with the United States than we ever had during the last half century.
Now I would like to say a word to my much respected friend, the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). He represented me as saying that I was content with the present situation-I think that is a correct quotation. I do not dissent from that idea, but when my hon. friend implies that to be content with the present situation is somewhat humiliating, and that is the real inference from his remarks, I am going to put a question to him. I am content with the present situation, I plead guilty to that, but will my hon. friend be good enough to tell me what changes he wants?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I will answer the question. Before I made that statement I pointed out that the hon. gentleman had described us as a colony-he said we were practically a colony.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: A few moments later he said, "I am satisfied with the present situation." That is what I was criticising -not our present situation, but the fact that the hon. gentleman had described us as being a colony, and then his going on to assert that he was satisfied with our present situation as being a colony. I went on to say further that if the people of Canada thought we were still a colony they would not be satisfied with that situation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am satisfied with the present situation-that is correct. But the present situation-call it what you like-[DOT] has not been changed. The constitution of Canada is the British North America Act, and amid all this talk of nationality and change of status we have not changed one letter in the British North America Act. There is no change of status for Canada. I grant that in trade, in importance, and in population Canada stands higher than ever before in the eyes of the world, but from the national point of view and from the constitutional point of view there has been no change whatever. Now, my hon. friend for Red Deer took the ground, in his usual forceful way, that nationhood and the appointment of an ambassador necessarily implied the existence of sovereign power. He made that statement very strongly. The right hon. member for King's, N.S., I understood, practically admitted that as correct. "Yes," he said, "you can only appoint an ambassador through sovereign power." But if I correctly understood his argument, he said, "If the King, as advised by the Privy Council of Canada, recommends the appointment of an ambassador, that makes us a sovereign power." I think I did not misunderstand the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I did not put it that way.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Not in those words. The hon. member for Red Deer said that the appointment of an ambassador was the evidence of sovereign power. My hon. friend for King's, N.S., met that by saying, "Yes, I admit that in effect, but if the King be advised by the Privy Council of Canada to make that appointment, that constitutes us a sovereign power." If he did not mean that, then my hon. friend did not meet the argument at all. Why, every day of our lives we do things in the name of the King. Here is a volume of the statutes of Canada, on every page of which you will find, "His Majesty by and with the advice of the Parliament of Canada," does so and so. Does that make us a sovereign power? The King is present in all oui courts; in every official action we use the name of the King. But surely that does not make us a sovereign power. The argument of the hon. member for Red Deer that an ambassador can receive his appointment only frofn a sovereign power is absolutely sound, and it has not been met by my hon. friend from King's.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve made one or two remarks on which I should like

to comment. Speaking of the future, he said, that the time will come when the ripened fruit will fall off. That illustration was given fifty years ago or more by a party in England, sometimes called the Little England party, who held that it was the natural development of these colonies that they should drop off with the ripening of the fruit. But strange to say, with the process of time, though the fruit ripens better than ever before, it does not drop off. Indeed, I think nearly every one will agree with me that the more the fruit ripens the more strongly it is attached to the stem than at any time in our history. I remember a good many years ago in my boyhood days-I am afraid to tell you how long ago it was-when the Prince of Wales, afterwards King Edward, came to Canada, a local bard in my town welcomed the Prince in three or four verses, only one of which I can recall. I am not so sure that it is to my credit to be able to quote it, bat one thing which has been flitting through my mind is the verse in which he was thinking of the possibility of the future. The hon. member for Maisonneuve said, ''We do not know what is going to happen in the future." That is true. It is the present and that portion of the future which is easily visible that we should deal with to-day, and we can only legislate and devise measures for it. This local bard evidently had that thought in his mind when he wrote these lines:
The changes time may bring
Par from our thoughts we fling.
Join we this day to sing,
God Save the King.
That is the true position. That is our position to-day. Changes may come, the . world moves on, and which one of us can say what will happen in the future? But we say as to the things of to-day and as to the things of the early future which are within our vision, that we ought to be content with our present situation as a portion of the British Empire, with all the local self-government we desire, and with, I think nothing to complain of.
I am sorry my hon. friend from Durham has gone, because I would like to have him present while I comment on his speech. I was surprised that so able a lawyer should endeavour to attach qualifications to the power of the British Parliament. My right hon. friend the Minister of Justice on a previous occasion had said, as quoted today by the hon. member for Beauce, that we are now in a position of equality with Great Britain. I was referring to that, and
I asked the hon. member for Durham, "As to the Parliament at Westminster in which we are not represented, has it not the power to wipe out the constitution of Canada-the British North America Act?" My hon. friend from Durham proceeded to argue that, strictly speaking, he did not propose to deny the power, but he said the British Parliament had not the right to do it. He talked a good deal about constitutional right. Well, right and power are not necessarily the same thing. We are constantly called upon to do things in this House which some of us think are not right, and power has to be exercised. In the discussion of our public affairs we on this side of the House, possibly erroneously, at all events in the exercise of our right of independent thought, have advanced certain propositions against the Government. We say that the Government has no right to do certain things. The answer is that the thing is done. They may have power to do it; we may have the right to declare they are wrong. But when the hon. member for Durham fails to recognize the distinction between right and power I think he is begging the question. I do not need to be a lawyer to say,-any one who has knowledge of the British system of Government must admit it-that there is absolutely no limitation to the power of the British Parliament. As one of our constitutional writers has said, "the only thing that Parliament cannot do is to make a man a woman." But in so far as any human effort can be made, the Parliament of Great Britain is supreme.
Now, all this talk of nationhood, of equality with Great Britain is absolutely unwarranted, and it is an impossible condition. I am only going to detain the committee two or three minutes longer while I quote one or two authorities. The hon. member for Durham cited Sir Frederick Pollock, arguing practically that while it was in the power of the British Parliament to do certain things, it would not do them. I am going to read one or two authorities as a contribution to the literature of this discussion. I do not think this time is wasted. I think the discussion to-day as dealing with a very important question has been an illuminating discussion and I think we ought to be pleased, although we differ in some respects, that it has taken place. But in answer to this story of the equality of Canada with other nations. I am going to give a quotation from no less authority than Lord Macaulay. I am not quoting from

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I should like
to say a word in reply to the arguments which my hon. friend has addressed to the committee. I join with him and with other members in appreciation of the spirit in which this debate has been carried on. My hon. friend might well have added one further illustration to those which he gave in the concluding portion of his speech; he might have added that His Majesty the King has absolute power to veto every Act passed by the Imperial Parliament. So far as the power is concerned, it is there; if the King does not assent to an Act of the Imperial Parliament it has no effect. The Act is brought into being, into effective operation, by the consent of the King, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons. If the King sees fit to veto or to withhold his assent, then the Act has no operation. Mr. Asquith said some years ago that the exercise of that power to veto had not been known since the time of Queen Anne, and that the power itself was as dead as Queen Anne. The Parliament of the United Kingdom has legal power to make a tariff for this country. It had power during the war through which we have just passed to pass an Act for compulsory military service in Canada. It had abso-
12 m. lutely no constitutional right to do either of these things. If my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's

will look at the works, recent and otherwise, of Lord Bryce, of President Lowell of Harvard, of Mr. Dicey, of Mr. Anson, and of half a dozen other constitutional writers whom I could name and from whom I could quote if it were worth while, he would find that legal power in the constitution of the British Empire is absolutely limited by constitutional right; therefore when he makes the suggestion that he has put forward here he is quite at sea so far as the opinion of great constitutional writers and of the leading statesmen of the country is concerned. Further than that, when my hon. friend suggests that if there had been no change in the British North America Acts this Dominion would have precisely the same status that it had on the first day of July, 1867, he is absolutely beside the mark. The British North America Act has had its meaning, its scope and its effect modified during all these years, by that very constitutional usage to which I have just now alluded and which has so profoundly affected the methods of government in the United Kingdom. All these things are the mere commonplaces of constitutional history and constitutional law, and I am rather surprised that my hon. friend should have put forward in seriousness some of the suggestions which he has addressed to this committee.
Now, the hon. gentleman has endeavoured to involve me in some dilemma in regard to the answer which I made to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I said in reply to the hon. member for Red Deer that the appointment of the proposed minister was to be made by the King, who is as much the King of Canada as he is of the British Isles and who acts within this Dominion of Canada upon the advice of the King's Privy Council for Canada. I pointed out further that no one, I suppose, who has given any consideration to the question will deny, that what is called the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission is really a Canadian section. It is called the Canadian section, and it is the Canadian section. It is an international commission and the United States under that treaty are dealing internationally and we are dealing internationally. Does any hon. gentleman in this House suggest the contrary of that? And how are these commissioners appointed? Precisely in the same way in which it is proposed to appoint this minister-by His Majesty the King, acting upon a nomination made by
the King's Privy Council for Canada. Is there any distinction between the two cases? Have I made myself clear to hon. gentlemen in this committee? That is the answer which I intended to give to my hon. friend from Red Deer and that is the answer which I now give to my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's. So far as sovereign power is concerned, my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, has quoted from Oppenheim, whose authority I recognize. I have quotations under my hand from Oppenheim which show that in foreign affairs considerations may apply which are already recognized in domestic affairs. It has been repeatedly pointed out that the same King acts by the advice of his Parliament in Great Britain, by the advice of his Parliament in Canada and by the advice of his Legislature in every province of Canada. Then is not sovereignty divisible so far as domestic relations are concerned? I should like to tell the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's that there is good ground in the opinion of some constitutional writers, to hold that sovereignty in respect of foreign relations is also divisible in somewhat the same sense. Whether that be true or not there is no question about it in this case, because the minister who is to be charged specially with the interests of Canada in relation to the United States will be appointed by His Majesty the King of the whole Empire and therefore the King of Canada, upon the nomination and recommendation of the King's Privy Council for Canada.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

speechtext: There is just one illustration that my right hon. friend gave, to which I wish to call attention, because it is one that we can all readily understand. He said that the Parliament of, Great Britain cannot make a tariff for Canada. The Parliament of Great Britain, he said, could not authorise conscription in Canada. My right hon. friend was wrong. The Parliament of Great Britain could do both. Why is it that they did not do both? Because they had, in the exercise of their power, delegated, through the British North America Act, all these powers to the people of Canada. It is an illustration of the power which exists in the Imperial Parliament delegated to this Parliament through the British North America Act.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: But the reason that that could not be done is the reason that I gave a moment ago, that, in this respect as in other respects which have governed the development and growth of government within the British Empire, legal power is absolutely controlled by constitutional right.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I have no desire to prolong this discussion; but I just want to say that I am utterly unconvinced by my right hon. friend's comparison between the appointment of an ambassador or a plenipotentiary to a foreign court and the case of an international commission, as it is called. In its application to Canada, it is a domestic affair; it is looking after the interests of Canada in her domestic affairs, and the term "international" is applied to that commission simply because both nations have an interest in the matter that is going on. But when you appoint an ambassador to a foreign court, you take the position of a sovereign state, and I ask my right hon. friend to contradict me if I am wrong when I say that no plenipotentiary or ambassador to a foreign power has ever been appointed except by a sovereign state. He knows very well what the meaning of the term sovereign state is.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not know that I can make myself any plainer to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) than I have already done. It is apparent,
I should think, that a section of the commission, appointed under a treaty made between two countries foreign to each other, must have another relation and scope than that which he described as purely domestic. Their action is not limited to this country; the commission operates and has jurisdiction in Canada; it operates and hns jurisdiction in the United States. The powers and duties vested in the Commission can only be carried out by the commission as a whole, consisting of two sections, one of them appointed by the United States and the other appointed by Canada through the medium of His Majesty the King acting upon the advice of the King's Privy Council

for Canada. Therefore, I venture to repeat, with all respect to my hon. friend, that so far as my opinion goes, the two cases depend precisely upon the same principle and that if you admit, as you must admit, that the principle is properly applied in the one case, you must, of necessity, also admit that it can be equally applied in the other.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am going to ask my right hon. friend-he knows very well-the question: Is Canada a sovereign state? That is the first question. He can answer that question. The second one I want him to answer is this: In case Canada is not a sovereign state, am I right in saying that this is a totally new departure inasmuch as a plenipotentiary or ambassador has never been appointed except by a sovereign state?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: My hon. friend has put a question which I shall be very glad to answer. Canada, as one of the nations of the Empire, owes allegiance to His Majesty the King who unquestionably is sovereign in respect of the whole Empire and sovereign therefore in each Dominion of the Empire. In each Dominion he acts only upon the advice of his ministers for that Dominion. Thus, the King is sovereign in Canada, and Canada in respect of its allegiance to the King and in respect of its status as a nation in the British Empire, is sovereign in this essential respect that the King, having regard to the special interest of Canada, has an absolute and perfect right on the advice of his Canadian ministers to appoint a plenipotentiary to concern himself specially with the affairs of Canada in relation to any foreign country.

speechtext: I would like to understand the difference between this item and No. 88: Allowance to active militia. We passed an item of $120,000 for allowance. There seems to be something of the same character here. How do these differ from one another?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Is there a grant for pipe
bands?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am informed they get precisely the same, $180,000.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
In respect to the rifle
associations to which the minister has referred, are any of them civilian organizations ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, prior to the war civilian associations were recognized and considered and grants made to them, but since the war the civilian associations have not yet been revived. I expect that a number of them will be revived during the course of the coming summer, and, of course, they are entitled to use, and do use, the military rifle ranges where they exist. The grants to the associations included in this vote are-Dominion Rifle Association, $35,000; the Provincial Rifle Associations, $13,600; University Rifle Association,

$1,000; and local rifle associations, whether civilian or belonging to military units, $40,000.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
what conditions are required of these rifle associations, whether military or civilian, before they obtain a grant?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The civilian rifle association before it is entitled to a grant must-have a membership of fifty. There is a membership of fifty required in the military unit too, I understand. In the military service the ammunition for rifle practice is issued free of charge; the civilian associations receive it at very much reduced charge.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Are there any regulations with regard to the place where the shooting is to be carried on, the season of the year, supervision and so on?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Yes, there are established regulations which have been in force for a number of years-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: What about supervision?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: -and then the grant is paid on a report from an inspecting officer.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The inspecting officer of
the district, I presume, in which the shooting is done?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It is the local district
officer where the association is that makes the report.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Maintenance, $200,000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: This is the maintenance of our military properties which are provided with fuel, light, water, telephone, rents and sanitary services in connection with the buildings. There are also armouries, store rooms, and rifle ranges owned or rented by the Government, except those of the Permanent Force. I think the item has been at this figure for a considerable time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: This has nothing to do with the salaries of caretakers, etc?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Does the drill hall in Ottawa belong to the Permanent Force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The buildings and
barracks of the Permanent Force are not included in this vote.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Are there any drill halls, armouries, and rifle ranges which belong exclusively to the Permanent Force in Canada ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The buildings occupied by the Permanent Force are known as barracks, and the armouries and drill halls are for the use of the militia units.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Is there another item for that purpose? If so, where do we find it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am informed it is in the vote of six and a-quarter millions for the Permanent Force. Item N >. 102, a little farther down, includes the upkeep of barracks.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Ordnance arms, lands, $75,000.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The ten minutes has now run into fifteen.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Too much is plenty.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Might I ask my hon. friends to consider this one item? It is desired that items 101 and 102 should stand over anyway, but I think we should pass the present item. It is $25,000 less than last year.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
This is for ordnance
arms, lands, etc. A little further down in the list appears an item for warlike stores. There may be some discussion and I think the minister should really let the item stand over.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Well, I have no objection. If my fion. friend desires to discuss this I will move that the committee rise and report progress and beg leave to sit again.	-
Item stands.
Progress reported.
On motion of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, the House adjourned at 12.50 a.m., Friday.
Friday, April 22, 1921.
